The Atacama Desert is a desert plateau in South America, mainly in northern Chile, with some areas extending into southern Peru. It is often described as the driest non-polar desert in the world. Some weather stations in its interior have recorded no significant rainfall for years. The desert lies between the Pacific Ocean to the west and the Andes to the east, forming a narrow strip along the Pacific coast.

It covers about 105,000 square kilometres (41,000 sq mi), though some definitions include nearby arid lands. Its dryness comes from several factors: the cold Humboldt Current reduces evaporation and cloud formation offshore, the subtropical high-pressure system limits precipitation, and the Andes block moist air from the Amazon Basin. Much of the region gets only a few millimetres of rain each year, and some central areas may go decades without measurable rainfall.

Even in these conditions, the Atacama supports specialized plant and animal life. Vegetation is sparse in the driest areas, but cacti, shrubs, and grasses grow in less extreme parts of the desert. Coastal fog, known locally as camanchaca, provides moisture for some ecosystems. Wildlife includes insects, reptiles, birds, and mammals adapted to arid conditions, while high-altitude wetlands and salt flats support flamingos and other Andean species.

The desert has been inhabited for a long time by Indigenous peoples, including the Atacameño, or Likan Antai, who built settlements in oases and river valleys. Under European colonization, the region came under Spanish rule. In the 19th century it became economically important for deposits of nitrates, copper, and other minerals. Disputes over these resources helped lead to the War of the Pacific (1879–1884), after which Chile took control of large desert territories that had been held by Peru and Bolivia.

Today the Atacama remains a major mining region, especially for copper and lithium. It is also one of the world's leading sites for astronomy. High elevation, low humidity, minimal cloud cover, and limited light pollution make it well suited to astronomical observation. Major observatories in or near the region include the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and facilities on Cerro Paranal and La Silla.

The Atacama is also a destination for tourism and scientific research. Its landscape includes salt flats, volcanoes, geysers, and eroded rock formations. Because its dry conditions resemble those on Mars, researchers have used the desert as a testing ground for space exploration technology and for studies of life in extreme environments.

Moving to a new city can feel, at first, like stepping into a life meant for someone braver than you. The reason for the move may sound simple enough: a job, school, a relationship, or just the feeling that you need a change. On paper, it looks neat. In real life, it means cardboard boxes, forwarded mail, a GPS voice telling you where to turn, and the strange feeling of waking up in a room where even the light looks unfamiliar. The good parts and the hard parts show up at the same time, and it’s hard to pull them apart.

One of the best parts of a new city is the chance to see yourself differently. In the place you’ve always lived, your identity can start to feel fixed. You are someone’s child, someone’s friend, the person who orders the usual coffee or avoids certain streets because they carry old memories. In a new city, nobody knows your history unless you decide to share it. That anonymity can feel lonely, but it can also feel freeing. You can be more outgoing, or quieter. You can try new routines, new neighborhoods, even new ways of being. The city does not care who you used to be. It asks only how you will live there now.

There is also the plain pleasure of discovery. In a new city, ordinary errands can feel like exploration. Buying groceries becomes its own small trip. You notice the buildings, the slang, the weather, the way people stand in line or talk to strangers. You learn where to get good bread, which park is quiet at dusk, which train platform crowds first when it rains. These details build slowly, and each one makes the place feel less foreign and more like home. Moving reminds you that daily life is not as fixed as it can seem.

But the costs are real, and they are often harder to measure than rent or moving expenses. The clearest one is homesickness, though that word can sound too gentle for what it really means. Homesickness is not just missing people. It is also missing the version of yourself that fit easily around them. In your old city, you knew how to belong without thinking about it. In the new one, belonging takes effort. You have to build a life almost from scratch: find a doctor, a mechanic, a café you like, a person to call when something breaks. Even simple errands can wear you out when nothing feels familiar yet.

Then there is the math of distance. Moving often means accepting that love becomes less convenient. Friendships that once depended on proximity now rely on texts, scheduled calls, and expensive visits. Family milestones happen without you, or you come back to find that home kept changing while you were gone. The place you left does not stay preserved for your return. It keeps moving, just as you do. There is grief in that.

Still, that may be part of what makes moving worth it. A life often grows by being unsettled. A new city offers freedom, novelty, and growth, but it asks for uncertainty, loneliness, and loss in return. To move is to accept that trade. If you stay long enough, the strange streets start to feel like your streets. The losses do not vanish, but they begin to feel less like a punishment and more like the cost of becoming bigger than the life you once knew.

A regional hospital network said Tuesday that it is investigating a data breach that may have exposed the personal and medical information of thousands of patients.

The network, which runs several hospitals, outpatient clinics, and specialty care centers, said it detected suspicious activity in its computer systems earlier this month. It said it moved to contain the incident, began an internal investigation, and brought in outside cybersecurity experts to determine the scope of the breach.

Early findings indicate that unauthorized actors may have accessed patient records with names, dates of birth, addresses, phone numbers, medical record numbers, insurance information, and, in some cases, limited clinical details. Hospital officials said they have found no evidence so far that financial account or payment card data was affected, but the investigation is still underway.

“We take the privacy and security of our patients’ information extremely seriously,” the network said in a statement. “Upon discovering this issue, we immediately implemented containment measures, notified law enforcement, and began working with leading forensic specialists to assess what information may have been affected.”

The network did not say how many patients were affected but called the breach significant. It said patients who may have been affected are expected to receive notices by mail in the coming weeks. The organization also said it will offer free credit monitoring and identity protection services to eligible patients as a precaution.

Hospital operations have continued during the investigation, though some administrative systems were taken offline for a time, causing delays in scheduling and access to some online services. Emergency departments and inpatient care were not disrupted, officials said.

Healthcare organizations remain common targets for hackers because they store large amounts of sensitive personal and medical data. Unlike stolen credit card numbers, medical records can include permanent identifying information that can be used for identity theft, insurance fraud, or phishing.

“This type of incident can have long-lasting consequences for patients,” said a data privacy analyst not affiliated with the network. “Even if clinical care is unaffected, the loss of trust can be substantial, especially when health information is involved.”

Regulators are likely to review the breach under federal health privacy rules, including the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, or HIPAA, which requires covered entities to protect patient information and notify individuals when certain breaches occur.

Patients are being advised to watch for unexpected bills, insurance statements, or suspicious emails and phone calls related to their medical care. The hospital network said it is reviewing access controls, strengthening system security, and taking other steps to reduce the risk of a similar incident.

drafts:
A good teacher is not just someone who knows the subject. Knowledge matters, but by itself it does not spark curiosity, build confidence, or change a student’s life. What matters just as much is patience, enthusiasm, empathy, and the ability to make students feel noticed. The best teachers do more than explain material. They make learning feel possible.

Patience is one of the clearest signs of a good teacher. Students learn at different speeds, and they do not all think in the same way. A good teacher understands that. When a student struggles, they do not give up or show frustration. They try a different explanation, a better example, or a new approach. That kind of patience tells students that struggling is part of learning, not proof that they have failed. For students who already doubt themselves, that message can matter a lot. A patient teacher does not only teach the subject. They also teach persistence.

Passion matters too. Students can tell when a teacher cares about what they are teaching. Interest has a way of spreading. A teacher who genuinely enjoys literature, science, history, or math can make even a hard topic feel alive. That energy changes the mood of a classroom. Lessons stop feeling like a list of facts and start to feel worth paying attention to. Just as important, students begin to see that learning can be satisfying, not just required.

Empathy is just as important. A good teacher remembers what it is like to feel confused, anxious, or embarrassed about getting something wrong. They know students often bring other worries into the room: problems at home, stress, insecurity, loneliness, or pressure to succeed. So they treat students with patience and respect. They listen. They notice when someone has gone quiet or seems discouraged. Sometimes the most helpful thing a teacher can offer is not another explanation, but a word of encouragement at the right time. Students who feel understood are more likely to speak up, take risks, and trust that they can improve.

Good teachers also know when to push. Being kind does not mean expecting less. Often the most effective teachers ask a lot of their students because they can see what those students are capable of. They push them to think harder, work more carefully, and aim higher than they would on their own. The difference is that they do not leave students there by themselves. High expectations work best when they come with support.

A good teacher can leave a mark that lasts long after the class ends. Years later, students may not remember every lesson, date, or formula, but they often remember how a teacher made them feel. They remember the teacher who believed in them when they were unsure, who opened up an interest they had never considered, or who made them feel that their voice mattered. Teaching is not only about passing on information. It is also about helping students grow into themselves.

To me, a good teacher is someone who combines knowledge with humanity. They guide, challenge, encourage, and inspire. They help students learn about the world, and about themselves. That kind of influence can last a lifetime.

# Commit message style guide

Good commit messages make reviews easier, leave useful history, and help when you are tracking down a change with `git log` or `git blame`. Use these conventions for every commit.

## Structure

```
<subject line>

<body>

<footer>
```

Put a blank line between the subject and the body. The body and footer are optional for small, obvious changes.

## Subject line

- **Keep it under 50 characters.** Do not go past 72.
- **Use the imperative mood:** `Add retry logic`, not `Added retry logic` or `Adds retry logic`. A simple test: the subject should complete the sentence, `If applied, this commit will…`
- **Capitalize the first word.**
- **Do not end with a period.**
- **Be specific.** `Fix bug` and `Update code` are too vague. `Fix null check in user lookup` is better.

If your team uses prefixes such as `feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, or `refactor:`, use them consistently and keep the full subject within the length limit.

## Body

Use the body to explain **what changed and why**, not how. The diff already shows how. Useful things to cover include:

- What problem led to this change?
- Why this approach instead of another one?
- What side effects or limits should reviewers know about?

Wrap lines at 72 characters. For short lists, use hyphens or asterisks.

## Footer

Use the footer for metadata such as:

- Issue references: `Fixes #123`, `Refs #456`
- Breaking changes: `BREAKING CHANGE: description`
- Co-authors: `Co-authored-by: Name <email>`

## Scope

Keep each commit to one logical change. If the subject needs an `and`, consider splitting the commit. Do not mix formatting-only edits with functional changes unless there is a clear reason.

## Examples

**Weak:**
```
fixed stuff
```

**Strong:**
```
Fix race condition in session cleanup

The cleanup job could delete sessions that were being
refreshed at the same time, which logged users out.
Acquire a row-level lock before checking expiration.

Fixes #482
```

## Avoid

- Vague messages such as `WIP`, `misc fixes`, or `updates`
- Describing the file instead of the change
- Referring to context only you know, such as `as discussed`
- Blame or commentary, such as `fix stupid bug`
- Generated changes with no explanation

## Final check

Before you commit, ask: would someone reading this in two years understand why you made the change? If not, add the missing context.

# Tbilisi

**Tbilisi** (Georgian: თბილისი), historically known as **Tiflis**, is the capital and largest city of Georgia. It stands on the banks of the Mtkvari (Kura) River and had a population of about 1.2 million in the early 2020s, or roughly a third of the country's population. Tbilisi is the country's main cultural, economic, and transport center and the largest city in the South Caucasus.

## History

According to tradition, King Vakhtang I Gorgasali of Iberia founded the city in the 5th century AD after discovering the area's warm sulfur springs while hunting. The name comes from the Old Georgian *tbili*, meaning "warm." His successors moved the royal seat to Tbilisi, and the city grew despite repeated invasions by Persians, Byzantines, Arabs, Mongols, and Turkic dynasties.

Tbilisi reached a high point during the Georgian Golden Age under King David IV and Queen Tamar in the 12th and early 13th centuries. It was later sacked several times, including by Timur and by the Persian ruler Agha Mohammad Khan in 1795. After Georgia was annexed by the Russian Empire in the early 19th century, Tbilisi became the administrative center of the Caucasus Viceroyalty. Following a brief period of independence from 1918 to 1921, it became the capital of the Georgian Soviet Socialist Republic. Georgia regained independence in 1991, and Tbilisi has since seen political unrest, including the Rose Revolution of 2003, along with major redevelopment.

## Geography and climate

Tbilisi lies in a valley surrounded by mountains and hills, at an elevation of about 400 to 770 meters above sea level. Its climate is transitional between humid subtropical and continental, with hot summers and cool winters.

## Culture and architecture

Tbilisi is known for its mix of medieval, neoclassical, Art Nouveau, Soviet, and contemporary architecture. The Old Town (Dzveli Tbilisi) has narrow streets, carved wooden balconies, and the sulfur baths of Abanotubani. Major landmarks include Narikala Fortress, Metekhi Church, Sioni Cathedral, Holy Trinity Cathedral (Sameba), and the Bridge of Peace. The Kartlis Deda ("Mother of Georgia") statue stands above the city on Sololaki Ridge.

The city has many theaters, museums, and festivals, including the Georgian National Museum and the Rustaveli Theatre. Georgian cuisine, including *khachapuri*, *khinkali*, and local wines, is central to the city's identity. Tbilisi's nightlife and electronic music scene have also drawn international attention.

## Economy and transport

Tbilisi is Georgia's financial and commercial center. Its main sectors include services, tourism, trade, and manufacturing. The Tbilisi Metro, opened in 1966, is the city's main rapid transit system, supported by buses, minibuses, and a cable car. Tbilisi International Airport is the country's main international gateway.

## See also

- Georgia (country)
- Kartli
- List of cities in Georgia

# Record turnout marks Tuesday's school board election in Maplewood County

Maplewood County drew its biggest turnout in decades for Tuesday's school board election, with 41 percent of registered voters casting ballots.

The County Elections Office said 38,214 of the district's 93,200 registered voters took part, up from about 17 percent in the last school board election two years ago. Officials said it was the highest turnout for a stand-alone local race in county records.

Several precincts reported lines out the door during the after-work rush. At Lincoln Elementary, polls stayed open 25 minutes past the scheduled 7 p.m. closing time so everyone already in line could vote.

"We prepared for a busy day, but nothing like this," said Dolores Whitfield, the county's elections director. "By noon we had already surpassed the total in-person turnout from the last cycle."

The race centered on a proposed budget shortfall, school consolidation plans, curriculum, and class sizes. Six candidates ran for three open seats. The campaign also drew heavier spending than most local contests and filled candidate forums.

Parent groups on both sides of the consolidation debate organized door-knocking efforts and carpools to the polls. Student volunteers from Maplewood High School ran a fall registration drive that added nearly 1,800 voters to the rolls.

"I've lived here 30 years and never voted in a school board race until this year," said Marcus Delgado, 52, a father of two who waited about 20 minutes to vote at Lincoln Elementary. "Decisions about my kids' classrooms are being made, and I wanted a say."

"Closing a school affects the whole neighborhood, not just the families who go there," said Ruth Ann Kessler, a retired teacher.

Preliminary results show incumbent Priya Raman in the lead, followed by newcomers Thomas Berglund and Angela Ortiz for the other two seats. Fewer than 400 votes separated third and fourth place, and the elections office said results would not be certified until provisional and mail-in ballots are counted next week.

Whitfield said her office would review Election Day operations before the next high-turnout race.

The new board members will be sworn in at the first meeting of the new year.

# Record turnout marks Tuesday's school board election in Maplewood County

Residents of Maplewood County turned out in high numbers Tuesday to elect three members to the school board, with election officials reporting that 41 percent of registered voters cast ballots. The County Elections Office said 38,214 of the district's 93,200 registered voters participated, compared with roughly 17 percent two years ago. Six candidates competed for three open seats, and the race drew unusually large campaign spending for a local contest, along with a series of packed candidate forums.

Parent groups on both sides of the consolidation debate organized door-knocking efforts and carpools to the polls. Student volunteers from Maplewood High School also ran a registration drive in the fall that added nearly 1,800 new voters to the rolls.

"I've lived here 30 years and never voted in a school board race until this year," said Marcus Delgado, 52, a father of two who waited about 20 minutes to vote at Lincoln Elementary. "Decisions about my kids' classrooms are being made, and I wanted a say."

Others said the high stakes brought them out. "Closing a school affects the whole neighborhood, not just the families who go there," said Ruth Ann Kessler, a retired teacher.

Preliminary results show incumbent Priya Raman leading the field, followed by newcomers Thomas Berglund and Angela Ortiz, who currently hold the other two winning positions. The margin between third and fourth place was fewer than 400 votes, and the elections office said final results will not be certified until provisional and mail-in ballots are counted next week.

Whitfield said her office would review the day's operations to prepare for future high-turnout elections. "This is a good problem to have," she said. "We hope it's a sign of lasting engagement."

The new board members will be sworn in at the first meeting of the new year.

Voyager 1 is a robotic space probe operated by NASA. It launched on 5 September 1977 as part of the Voyager program to study the outer Solar System. After finishing its original mission, it continued outward and is now the most distant human-made object from Earth.

The Jet Propulsion Laboratory built Voyager 1, and a Titan IIIE rocket launched it from Cape Canaveral, Florida. Although Voyager 2 launched first, Voyager 1 followed a faster path and reached Jupiter and Saturn earlier. Its mission used a rare planetary alignment that let spacecraft visit multiple outer planets through gravitational assists.

Voyager 1 made its first major encounter with Jupiter in 1979. During the flyby, it returned detailed images of the planet's atmosphere, including its cloud bands and the Great Red Spot. It also found evidence of active volcanism on Io, the first volcanic activity observed beyond Earth. The probe also gathered data on Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto, along with Jupiter's magnetosphere and ring system.

In 1980, Voyager 1 flew past Saturn and its moon Titan. Titan was a priority because of its dense atmosphere. The spacecraft confirmed that the atmosphere is rich in nitrogen, though its thick haze blocked clear views of the surface. Voyager 1 also returned observations of Saturn's rings, moons, and magnetic environment. Because the Titan flyby required a different path, the spacecraft left the plane of the Solar System and could not continue to other planets.

After the planetary mission, Voyager 1 began an extended mission to study the outer heliosphere, the region shaped by the solar wind. ## Pivot Tables User Guide

A pivot table summarizes and analyzes spreadsheet data without requiring you to sort it by hand or write a set of formulas. You can use it to group data, calculate totals, and compare categories.

### When to Use a Pivot Table
Use a pivot table when you need to:
- Total sales by region, product, or salesperson
- Count records such as customers or orders
- Compare values across categories
- Rearrange a summary without changing the original data
- Review patterns in a large dataset

### Before You Begin
Your source data should:
- Be arranged in rows and columns
- Have one header row
- Contain no completely blank rows or columns
- Use one data type per column, such as dates, numbers, or text

Example columns might include `Date`, `Region`, `Product`, `Salesperson`, `Units`, and `Revenue`.

### Creating a Pivot Table
1. Select any cell in the data range.
2. Open the **Insert** menu and choose **Pivot Table**.
3. Confirm the data range.
4. Choose where to place the pivot table:
   - New worksheet
   - Existing worksheet
5. Click **Create** or **OK**.

A blank pivot table and a field list will appear.

### Understanding the Pivot Table Areas
Most pivot-table tools include four areas:

- **Rows**: Shows categories vertically
- **Columns**: Shows categories horizontally
- **Values**: Shows calculations such as sum, count, or average
- **Filters**: Limits which data appears

### Building a Basic Pivot Table
To show total revenue by region:
1. Drag **Region** to **Rows**.
2. Drag **Revenue** to **Values**.

The pivot table will list each region with its total revenue.

To compare revenue by region and product:
1. Keep **Region** in **Rows**.
2. Drag **Product** to **Columns**.
3. Keep **Revenue** in **Values**.

### Changing Calculations
A value field can usually be summarized in several ways:
- Sum
- Count
- Average
- Minimum
- Maximum

To change the calculation:
1. Click the value field in the pivot table or field settings.
2. Open **Value Field Settings** or **Summarize By**.
3. Choose the calculation you want.

### Filtering and Sorting
You can narrow or reorder the results by:
- Applying a report filter, such as one year
- Sorting row labels alphabetically or by value
- Expanding or collapsing grouped items

### Refreshing the Pivot Table
If the source data changes, refresh the pivot table:
1. Click anywhere in the pivot table.
2. Select **Refresh** from the pivot-table toolbar or context menu.

### Tips
- Use clear column names
- Format numbers for readability, such as currency or percentages
- If dates do not group correctly, make sure they are stored as actual dates
- Leave the source data as is and use the pivot table for analysis

Pivot tables let you change how data is grouped and summarized in a few clicks, which makes reporting easier.

# Pivot Tables: A User Guide

## What Is a Pivot Table?

A pivot table helps you summarize a large set of data without writing formulas. You can group, count, total, and average your data, then rearrange it to answer different questions. For example: total sales by region, or orders closed by each rep each month.

## Before You Begin

Set up your data first:

- **Include headers:** Each column should have a unique, nonblank name.
- **Avoid blank rows or columns:** Blank spaces can cause the pivot table to miss part of the data.
- **Keep each column consistent:** A column should hold one kind of data only, such as dates, numbers, or names.

## Creating a Pivot Table

1. Click any cell in your data range.
2. Open the **Insert** menu and choose **Pivot Table**.
3. Check that the selected data range is correct.
4. Choose where to place the pivot table: a new sheet or an existing location.
5. Click **OK** or **Create**.

A blank pivot table will appear, along with a field panel that lists your column headers.

## Understanding the Four Areas

The field panel has four main areas. You build the report by dragging fields into each one.

- **Rows:** Categories shown down the left side, such as Product.
- **Columns:** Categories shown across the top, such as Quarter.
- **Values:** The numbers being calculated, such as Sum of Revenue.
- **Filters:** Fields that limit the entire table to certain items, such as one year.

## Example

Suppose your data includes Region, Salesperson, Month, and Revenue. To show revenue by region and month:

1. Drag **Region** to Rows.
2. Drag **Month** to Columns.
3. Drag **Revenue** to Values.

The pivot table will show total revenue for each region and month, with grand totals at the edges.

## Changing the Calculation

Numeric fields are usually summed by default. To change that, click the field in the Values box, open **Value Field Settings**, and choose another option such as Count, Average, Max, or Min. You can also show values as a percentage of the total.

## Refining Your Report

- **Sort:** Click the dropdown arrow next to a row or column label.
- **Filter:** Use the same arrow to hide selected items.
- **Group:** Right-click dates to group them by month, quarter, or year.
- **Rearrange:** Drag fields between areas to change the view.

## Keeping Data Current

Pivot tables usually do not update automatically when the source data changes. Right-click the table and choose **Refresh**. If you added new rows, you may also need to update the source range under **Change Data Source**.

## Troubleshooting

- **Numbers are counted instead of summed:** The column may contain text or blank cells. Clean the data, then refresh the table.
- **Dates won't group:** Some entries may be stored as text instead of real dates. Convert them, then try again.

Pivot tables are one of the quickest ways to make sense of a large dataset.

# Pivot Tables: A User Guide

## What Is a Pivot Table?

A pivot table summarizes large datasets without requiring formulas. It lets you group, count, total, and average your data, then rearrange it in seconds to view it from different angles. Use one when you need answers like "What were total sales by region?" or "How many orders did each rep close per month?"

## Before You Begin

Make sure your data is ready:

- Include headers: every column needs a unique, nonblank title.
- Avoid blank rows or columns: these can cause the table to miss data.
- Keep data consistent: each column should contain one type of information, such as dates or numbers only.

## Creating a Pivot Table

1. Click any cell inside your data range.
2. Open the **Insert** menu and choose **Pivot Table**.
3. Confirm the data range shown is correct.
4. Choose a destination: a new sheet (recommended) or an existing location.
5. Click **OK** or **Create**.

An empty pivot table appears, along with a field panel listing your column headers.

## Understanding the Four Areas

The field panel contains four boxes. Drag fields into them to build your report.

- Rows: categories listed down the left side, for example Product.
- Columns: categories listed across the top, for example Quarter.
- Values: the numbers being calculated, for example Sum of Revenue.
- Filters: fields that let you limit the whole table to specific items, such as a single year.

## Example

Suppose your data has columns for Region, Salesperson, Month, and Revenue. To see revenue by region and month:

1. Drag **Region** to Rows.
2. Drag **Month** to Columns.
3. Drag **Revenue** to Values.

The table now displays total revenue for each region-month combination, with grand totals along the edges.

## Changing the Calculation

By default, numeric fields are summed. To change this, click the field in the Values box, select **Value Field Settings**, and choose another function, such as Count, Average, Max, or Min. You can also display values as a percentage of the total.

## Refining Your Report

- Sort: click the dropdown arrow beside a row or column label.
- Filter: use the same arrow to uncheck items you want to hide.
- Group: right-click dates to group them by month, quarter, or year.
- Rearrange: drag fields between areas to see the data differently.

## Keeping Data Current

Pivot tables don't update automatically when source data changes. Right-click the table and select **Refresh**. If you've added new rows, you may need to update the source range under **Change Data Source**.

## Troubleshooting

- Numbers counted instead of summed: the column likely contains text or blanks. Clean the data and refresh.
- Dates won't group: some entries may be stored as text. Convert them to true dates.

With a little practice, pivot tables become one of the fastest ways to analyze data.

When I was nine, my grandmother took me to the train station in the town where she grew up. It had been closed for decades. The windows were clouded, and the brass was gone from the ticket counter. But she put her palm against the waiting-room wall as if she were checking for a pulse. “I left for the city from this bench,” she said. “Your grandfather proposed on that platform.” By any architectural standard, it was an unremarkable building. To her, it was where her life turned.

I think about that day whenever someone says old buildings are just obstacles: expensive to maintain, hard to retrofit, in the way of something newer. The case isn't silly. Old buildings leak. Wiring them is difficult. They often don't meet current codes, and nostalgia doesn't pay for a roof. I don't think every old structure should be saved. Survival alone doesn't make a building worth keeping.

But some are worth keeping, and not only for sentimental reasons.

First, old buildings preserve a kind of memory that no archive can. A photograph shows you how a street looked; a building lets you step into the scale people once lived with. You notice the low ceilings, the narrow stairs, the way light came through windows instead of switches. History stops feeling abstract when you have to duck through its doorway.

Second, they preserve workmanship we've mostly stopped paying for. In the library in my hometown, a hundred-year-old building where I spent a lot of time as a teenager, someone had carved tiny acorns into the banister. No one had to do that. No budget meeting would approve it now. But generations of bored kids ran their hands over those acorns, and I think it taught us, without anyone saying so, that ordinary places could still be made carefully.

Third, old buildings give a place continuity. Neighborhoods built entirely from new construction can feel strangely weightless, like sets waiting for actors. Older buildings make a place feel inhabited. They give newcomers and lifelong residents a landmark in common, even if they remember it differently. That matters. It's easier to tear a social fabric than to weave one.

Then there's the simpler issue of waste. As preservationists often point out, the greenest building is often the one already there. Demolition throws away the energy and materials already built into a structure, and it fills landfills too.

The train station was eventually replaced by a parking lot. Last year I drove through town and tried to find where the bench had been. I couldn't. The asphalt was smooth, the painted lines were crisp, and nothing suggested that anyone had once left from there, or been proposed to there.

That's what I'd want skeptics to understand. We don't preserve buildings because stone and timber are inherently precious. We preserve them because they keep the places where lives were shaped. Once they're gone, the bench is gone too. So is the hand on the wall, and the proof that any of it happened.

When I was nine, my grandmother took me to the train station in the town where she grew up. It had been closed for decades. The windows were clouded, and the brass was gone from the ticket counter. But she pressed her palm flat against the wall of the waiting room as though checking a sleeping animal for breath. “I left for the city from this bench,” she said. “Your grandfather proposed on that platform.” By any architectural standard, it was an unremarkable building. To her, it was where her life turned.

I think about that moment whenever someone argues that old buildings are simply obstacles, expensive to maintain and inconvenient to retrofit, standing where something shinier could go. The argument isn't foolish. Old buildings leak. Wiring them is difficult. They often don't meet current codes, and sentiment alone won't pay for a new roof. The Battle of Hastings was fought on 14 October 1066 between the forces of William, Duke of Normandy, and King Harold Godwinson of England. It was the decisive battle of the Norman Conquest of England and led to the establishment of Norman rule. Although it takes its name from the nearby town of Hastings, the battle was fought about 7 miles (11 km) to the northwest, near the present town of Battle in East Sussex.

The battle grew out of a dispute over the English throne. After Edward the Confessor died in January 1066, Harold Godwinson was crowned king. William of Normandy claimed that Edward had earlier promised him the throne and that Harold had sworn to support that claim. A third claimant, Harald Hardrada of Norway, also invaded England. Harold defeated and killed Hardrada at the Battle of Stamford Bridge on 25 September 1066, but the victory left his army tired.

William crossed the English Channel and landed at Pevensey on 28 September 1066. He then moved into Sussex, where he built a prefabricated castle at Hastings and raided the surrounding area, partly to draw Harold south. Harold advanced quickly from London with his household troops, the housecarls, and the shire levies known as the fyrd.

The two armies met on Senlac Hill. Harold's forces formed a dense shield wall along the ridge. William's army included infantry, archers, and cavalry. The battle lasted most of the day and was closely fought. Early Norman attacks were driven back by the English line. At one point, a rumor spread that William had been killed, but he is said to have lifted his helmet to show he was alive and to rally his men.

The battle turned when parts of the English line broke formation, possibly while pursuing retreating Normans. Historians still debate whether the retreats were real or feigned, but they let Norman cavalry isolate and destroy sections of Harold's army. Late in the day, Harold was killed. Tradition says he was struck in the eye by an arrow, though the exact manner of his death is uncertain. With the king dead and much of the English nobility killed, resistance collapsed.

William's victory cleared the way for his coronation as King William I of England on 25 December 1066. The conquest reshaped English society, the aristocracy, language, and government, and tied England more closely to continental Europe. It is also remembered through sources such as the Bayeux Tapestry, one of the main visual records of the conquest.

drafts:
Hundreds of thousands of commuters looked for other ways to get to work Monday after transit workers went on strike at dawn, shutting down bus and rail service across the region.

The Metro Transit Workers Union, which represents about 8,200 drivers, mechanics, and station staff, began the strike at 4 a.m. after contract talks with the Regional Transit Authority broke down late Sunday. It is the first systemwide stoppage in 14 years.

"We didn't want to be here," union president Dolores Reyes said on a picket line outside the Eastside bus depot. "But workers who keep this city moving can't be asked to fall behind on rent while costs rise every year."

The union wants a 9 percent wage increase over three years, stronger protections against assaults on drivers, and limits on mandatory overtime. Transit officials offered a 5 percent raise and said they could not meet the other demands without raising fares or cutting routes.

"Our offer was fair and fiscally responsible," Authority spokesperson Martin Vail said in a statement. "We remain at the table and urge the union to return to negotiations so riders can get back to their lives."

The effects showed up early. Highways were jammed before sunrise, and traffic officials reported delays as much as 70 percent longer than usual. Ride-share prices jumped, and bike-share stations downtown were empty by 8 a.m. Several major employers told staff to work from home.

At Central Station, where the morning crowd is usually dense, a few people stood reading closure notices. Marcus Hill, a hospital cafeteria worker, said he had walked two miles before a friend drove him the rest of the way.

"I support the drivers, I really do," Hill said. "But I can't afford to miss shifts either. I'm stuck in the middle."

Schools reported higher-than-usual absences. The district said yellow school buses would keep running because they are operated by a separate contractor. Paratransit service for riders with disabilities is running at limited capacity under an emergency agreement, though advocates said wait times had stretched past two hours.

Mayor Elaine Cho called on both sides to resume talks at once and offered city staff as mediators.

"Every day this continues costs working families and local businesses," she said.

Economists estimate the shutdown could cost the regional economy $30 million a day in lost productivity and sales.

No new negotiating session had been scheduled by Monday evening. The union said it would keep picketing until it received what it called a serious proposal. The Authority said it was making contingency plans for a prolonged stoppage.

drafts:
Some old buildings are worth saving for a simple reason: they still matter. Age by itself is not enough. A cracked wall or a faded sign does not become meaningful just because it lasted. But some buildings hold more than brick and stone. They carry memory, craft, identity, and traces of how people once imagined their lives. Saving them is not about freezing the past. It is about keeping a link between generations.

I think of old buildings as public memory. Families keep photo albums, letters, and heirlooms because objects can hold feeling in a way bare facts cannot. Cities and towns need their own versions of that. A preserved train station, schoolhouse, church, or row of apartments can reveal more about the people who built a place than any plaque can. The width of a staircase, the carved trim around a doorway, the wear on stone steps: these details show that history was lived with bodies, habits, and routine. Someone climbed those stairs every day. Someone stood in that hallway waiting for news, for work, for love, or for grief to ease. When buildings like that vanish, part of a community's memory goes with them.

They are also worth preserving because they offer a kind of beauty that is hard to replace. Many were built with patience, durable materials, and a level of care that came from pride rather than speed. Even modest buildings can show a human hand: uneven bricks laid one by one, wooden floors worn smooth by decades of footsteps, windows placed for grace as much as use. At a time when so much construction is shaped by speed and return, older buildings remind us that usefulness and beauty can coexist. They teach us to value texture, permanence, and detail.

There is an ethical case for preservation too. Demolition and rebuilding are not always signs of progress. Sometimes they are amnesia dressed up as development. Not every old building can or should be saved. Cities change, and communities need housing, safety, and access. But when a building has architectural character or deep cultural importance, preserving it becomes a form of respect. It says the people who came before us are not disposable, and that the struggles and achievements that shaped a neighborhood still count. That is especially true of places tied to ordinary people, not only the wealthy or famous. A factory, a corner store, or a union hall may tell a more democratic story than a mansion.

What stays with me most is the way preserved buildings make time feel layered rather than lost. To walk into an old library or courthouse is to feel, for a moment, that your life belongs to a longer human story. The building has outlasted fashions, governments, and private worries. It has seen generations pass through and still stands, asking for care, not pity. At its best, preservation is an act of humility. It acknowledges that we are not the first people to love a place, and not the last who will need something solid to remember it by.

In a time when so much construction is driven by speed and profit, these older buildings remind us that usefulness and beauty do not have to be enemies. They teach us to value texture, permanence, and detail.

There is also an ethical reason to preserve them. Demolishing and rebuilding is not always progress. Sometimes it is amnesia disguised as development. Of course, not every old building can or should be saved. Cities must change; communities need housing, safety, and accessibility. But when a building has architectural distinction or deep cultural importance, preservation becomes a form of respect. It says that the people who came before us are not disposable, and that the struggles and achievements that shaped a neighborhood still have meaning. This is especially true for places tied to ordinary people, not just the wealthy or famous. A factory, a corner store, or a union hall may tell a more democratic story than a mansion ever could.

To walk into an old library or courthouse is to feel, even briefly, that your own life is part of a longer human story. The building has outlasted fashions, governments, and private worries. It has witnessed generations and still stands, asking for care rather than pity. Preservation, at its best, is an act of humility. It admits that we are not the first people to love a place, and not the last who will need something solid to remember it by.

# Contributing to the docs

Thanks for helping improve the documentation. You can fix a typo, update a screenshot, write a tutorial, or review a pull request. Every contribution helps.

This guide covers the basics: how to set up the docs locally, make a change, and open a pull request.

## Ways to contribute

- **Fix errors:** typos, broken links, outdated screenshots, or incorrect code samples
- **Improve clarity:** rewrite confusing sections or add missing context
- **Write new content:** tutorials, how-to guides, and reference pages
- **Review pull requests:** a fresh read often catches problems the author missed
- **Report issues:** if you find a problem but can't fix it, open an issue

## Getting set up

1. **Fork** the repository and clone your fork locally.
2. Install dependencies with `npm install`.
3. Start the local preview server with `npm run dev`.
4. Open `http://localhost:3000` to preview your changes.

For small edits, you can also click **Edit this page** at the bottom of a page and make the change directly on GitHub.

## Making a change

1. Create a branch with a clear name, such as `fix-install-typo` or `add-auth-guide`.
2. Make your edits in the `docs/` directory. The files use Markdown.
3. Run `npm run lint` to check formatting, then run `npm run build` to make sure the site builds without broken links.
4. Commit with a clear message, such as `Fix incorrect flag in CLI reference`.
5. Push your branch and open a pull request.

## Style guidelines

Please follow these conventions:

- **Use plain language.** Prefer short sentences and avoid unnecessary jargon.
- **Address the reader as "you."**
- **Use active voice.** Write "Run the command," not "The command should be run."
- **Put code in code blocks** and specify the language for syntax highlighting.
- **Use sentence case** for headings.
- **Make examples runnable.** Test every snippet before you submit it.
- **Write descriptive link text.** Avoid "click here."

## Structure of the docs

The docs use four content types:

- **Tutorials:** step-by-step lessons for beginners
- **How-to guides:** solutions to specific problems
- **Reference:** technical descriptions
- **Explanations:** background and concepts

Try to keep each page focused on one type.

## Pull request checklist

Before you submit, confirm that:

- [ ] The site builds locally without errors.
- [ ] Links and code samples work.
- [ ] Your changes follow the style guidelines.
- [ ] The PR description explains what changed and why.

## Review process

A maintainer will usually respond within a few days. We may suggest edits before merging. That's a normal part of the process.

Once your pull request is approved, your changes are merged and published automatically.

## Community expectations

Be kind, patient, and respectful. All contributors must follow the Code of Conduct.

## Need help?

If you have a question, ask in the discussion forum or comment on an issue. We're glad to help, especially if this is your first contribution.

The Hanseatic League was a network of merchant guilds and market towns in northwestern and central Europe. From the late 12th century to the 17th, it controlled much of the trade in the Baltic and North Seas. At its peak, it linked nearly 200 towns, from London and Bruges to Novgorod and Bergen, and shaped the economy and growth of northern European cities.

The League grew out of the expansion of German merchants, especially from cities such as Lübeck and Hamburg, who wanted protection and trading privileges abroad. Lübeck, founded in 1143 and well placed between the North and Baltic Seas, became the League’s leading city. By the 13th century, merchants from German-speaking towns had set up trading outposts, or *Kontore*, in major foreign centers including London, Bruges, Bergen, and Novgorod. These outposts worked as warehouses, offices, and legal communities that defended Hanseatic interests.

The Hanseatic League was not a state. It had no formal constitution, permanent army, or central administration. It worked instead as a loose association of towns and merchants joined by shared commercial interests. Representatives of member cities met at assemblies called the *Hansetag* to negotiate trade policy, mutual defense, and relations with foreign rulers. Membership was flexible, and cities took part to different degrees.

Its strength came from the exchange of regional goods. Grain, timber, wax, fur, and fish moved west from the Baltic and eastern regions. Cloth, wine, salt, and metal goods came from the west and south. Hanseatic merchants built shipping networks and shared commercial practices that reduced costs and made long-distance trade more reliable. The League also used embargoes and, at times, naval force to protect its privileges, including in its conflicts with Denmark in the 14th century.

From the late 15th century, the League declined. Stronger territorial states, the shift of trade toward the Atlantic, competition from Dutch and English merchants, and internal divisions all reduced its influence. Its overseas privileges were gradually cut back, and several *Kontore* closed. Some cities continued to identify with the League, but by the 17th century its political role had mostly faded. The final meeting of the *Hansetag* was held in 1669.

The League still shaped the cities that had belonged to it. Lübeck, Hamburg, Bremen, and Tallinn, among others, retain brick Gothic buildings and civic traditions linked to the Hanseatic past. Historians often treat the League as an early example of commercial cooperation across borders and of networks formed by cities rather than states.

# Bike-share FAQ

## Getting started

**How do I rent a bike?**  
Download the app and create an account. Find a nearby station, tap "Unlock," and scan the bike's QR code. You can also unlock a bike at a station kiosk with a credit card.

**How much does it cost?**  
- **Single ride:** $1 to unlock, plus $0.15 per minute
- **Day pass:** $12 for unlimited 30-minute rides over 24 hours
- **Monthly membership:** $20 for unlimited 45-minute rides
- **Annual membership:** $150 for unlimited 45-minute rides

Discounted memberships are available for students, seniors, and low-income residents. Apply on our website.

## Using the service

**How long can I keep a bike?**  
You can ride as long as you want, but any time beyond your plan's included minutes is billed at $0.15 per minute. For longer trips, dock the bike and start a new ride to reset the clock.

**Where can I return my bike?**  
Return the bike to any station with an open dock. Push the front wheel firmly into the dock until the light turns green. If a station is full, use the app to find the nearest station with space. You'll get a free 10-minute extension.

**Do I need to bring a helmet?**  
Helmets are not provided, but we strongly recommend wearing one. Riders under 16 must wear a helmet by law.

**Are electric bikes available?**  
Yes. E-bikes have a green stripe and cost an extra $0.10 per minute. They provide pedal assist up to 20 mph.

## Safety and problems

**What if a bike is damaged?**  
Check the brakes, tires, and seat before you ride. If something looks wrong, press the red "Report" button on the bike's screen or report it in the app. Then return the bike to a dock so it can be taken out of service. You will not be charged for rides under one minute.

**What if the bike is lost or stolen?**  
Lock the bike with the built-in cable lock whenever you stop. For short stops, use the "Hold" feature in the app. If a bike is lost or stolen while checked out to you, report it within 24 hours. If you do not, you may be charged a $250 fee.

**Can I ride at night?**  
Yes. The bikes have front and rear lights that turn on automatically.

## Account help

**Can I share my membership?**  
No. Memberships are for one person, and each account can unlock only one bike at a time. Group rides require separate accounts.

**How do I cancel my membership?**  
Open Settings > Membership in the app and select "Cancel." Monthly plans end at the close of the billing period. Annual plans can be refunded within 14 days.

**Who do I contact for help?**  
Call 555-0142, email help@citybikeshare.example, or use the in-app chat. Support is available every day from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.

## Plugin system

The editor has a plugin system for extending its behavior without changing the main application. Plugins can add commands, sidebar panels, language support, formatters, themes, and event-based features.

### Plugin structure

Each plugin lives in its own directory and must include a manifest file named `plugin.json`. A typical plugin looks like this:

```text
my-plugin/
  plugin.json
  main.js
  README.md
  assets/
```

The `plugin.json` file defines the plugin's metadata and entry point:

```json
{
  "id": "example.hello-world",
  "name": "Hello World",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "main": "main.js",
  "enabled": true
}
```

Required fields:

- `id`: unique plugin identifier
- `name`: human-readable name
- `version`: plugin version
- `main`: entry script loaded by the editor

Optional fields include `description`, `author`, and `dependencies`.

### Lifecycle

When the editor starts, it scans the plugin directory, reads each manifest, and loads any plugin marked as enabled. The entry script must export an `activate` function. If the script also exports `deactivate`, the editor calls it when the plugin is unloaded or when the editor exits.

Example:

```js
export function activate(api) {
  api.commands.register("hello.sayHello", () => {
    api.window.showMessage("Hello from plugin!");
  });
}

export function deactivate() {
  // Clean up resources here
}
```

Use `activate` to register commands, subscribe to events, or set up UI elements. Use `deactivate` to clean up timers, listeners, and temporary state.

### Editor API

Plugins interact with the editor through the `api` object passed to `activate`. Common namespaces include:

- `api.commands`: register and run commands
- `api.window`: show notifications, dialogs, and UI panels
- `api.workspace`: access open files, project folders, and settings
- `api.editor`: read or modify the active document
- `api.events`: subscribe to events such as file open, save, or cursor movement

Example command registration:

```js
export function activate(api) {
  api.commands.register("example.insertDate", () => {
    const editor = api.editor.getActiveEditor();
    if (!editor) return;

    editor.insertText(new Date().toLocaleDateString());
  });
}
```

### Installation and management

Plugins can be installed by copying their directory into the editor's `plugins/` folder or by using the built-in plugin manager. Users can enable, disable, update, or remove plugins from the settings interface.

If a plugin fails to load, the editor logs the error and continues starting up. Load errors, activation failures, and dependency issues appear in the developer console.

### Best practices

- Keep each plugin focused on one job.
- Use stable, namespaced command IDs such as `author.feature.action`.
- Validate settings and handle missing editor state gracefully.
- Dispose of event listeners during deactivation.
- Avoid blocking work during activation so startup stays fast.

A good plugin should fit naturally into the editor, stay lightweight, and fail safely when the required context is missing.

Last summer my phone died on a train, and I had four hours of countryside ahead of me with nothing to do but look out the window. For the first twenty minutes I was almost frantic. My hand kept drifting to my pocket like a tongue to a missing tooth. I counted fence posts. I reread the safety instructions above the door. I was bored.

Then something changed. Somewhere after a river I couldn't name, my mind stopped reaching for input and started making its own. I remembered a conversation with my grandmother that I hadn't thought about in years. I figured out how to restructure a project at work that had been bothering me for weeks. I invented, for no reason, an elaborate backstory for the man asleep across the aisle. By the time we pulled into the station, I felt oddly rested, as if I'd been somewhere.

I think about that trip often because it showed me what I've been giving up. Boredom used to be unavoidable. It filled waiting rooms, long car rides, and the dead hour between homework and dinner. Now I can erase it almost completely. Every gap in the day can be filled with a feed, a podcast, a scroll. I've gotten so good at avoiding boredom that I almost forgot it had a use.

I think that use is a kind of mental housekeeping. When nothing is asking for our attention, the mind turns inward and starts sorting. It makes connections it might not make otherwise. It brings up worries we've been outrunning and wants we haven't admitted. Psychologists have linked this kind of idle wandering to creativity and planning, and that fits my experience. My best ideas never arrive while I'm taking something in. They come in the shower, on walks, while washing dishes, in the loose edges of the day.

Boredom can also teach desire. If I'm bored long enough, I find out what I actually want to do instead of what happens to be in front of me. As a kid, summer boredom eventually pushed me to build a fort, start a terrible comic, or take apart a broken radio. Nobody assigned me those projects. They came out of the discomfort of an empty afternoon, and they felt like mine in a way entertainment never does.

I don't want to overstate it. Boredom is unpleasant, and that's part of its value. It's a signal, like hunger, that something in us wants engagement. The mistake is answering that signal with whatever is closest. Fast food quiets hunger without nourishing you, and scrolling quiets boredom without giving the mind anything to work on.

So I've started practicing a small discipline. I leave my phone in my bag while I wait in line. I take walks without headphones. Sometimes I sit on the porch and watch the light change on the neighbor's maple. The first few minutes are always itchy. Then, almost every time, the restlessness gives way to something roomier, and thoughts I didn't know I was carrying begin to come up.

I used to think an empty moment was a wasted one. Now I think it may be more like fallow ground. It looks inactive, but it's where the next thing begins.

When I was nine, I watched my uncle slaughter a pig. I had been told to stay in the truck, and of course I didn’t. What stays with me is not the blood but the quiet afterward, how quickly the men returned to themselves, rinsing their hands and talking about the weather. That night we ate pork shoulder. It was delicious. I kept thinking about the pig’s eyes.

I’ve been coming back to that evening for most of my adult life.

For years I dodged the question. I ate chicken breasts sealed in plastic, trimmed into shapes that no longer looked like an animal. Then I read a book about industrial farming, the kind of book that ruins your appetite. It did. I became a vegetarian for three years. I meant it, and I was a little insufferable about it.

I believed then, and still do, that suffering matters. Pigs are intelligent, social animals. They feel fear. If I think a dog’s pain matters, I need some reason why a pig’s would not, and “because it tastes good” is not much of one. Most meat comes from animals raised in conditions I would call cruel if I saw them imposed on anything I loved. I don’t really know how to argue past that anymore.

What has changed is not the argument but my confidence in living by it cleanly. I spent one winter with relatives whose diet came mostly from what they raised and hunted, and their relation to meat was nothing like mine. They knew the animals. They thanked them without self-consciousness. They wasted nothing. I could not honestly say they were doing something worse than I was when I stood in a grocery store buying almond milk shipped from a drought-stricken valley. Every way of eating has a cost. The question is whether you are willing to see it.

That is where I seem to have arrived, though not comfortably. The worst part of modern meat is not death itself but how completely the death is hidden. Distance makes cruelty easier. If I am going to eat an animal, I should be willing to know where it lived and how it died. If I cannot bear to know, that tells me something too.

Now I eat meat rarely and try to know where it comes from. I buy from a farmer whose fields I have walked. Sometimes I fall short. I eat whatever is easiest at an airport or a wedding, and I feel the old pang. I do not think this makes me virtuous. It may only make me a more conscious participant in something I still cannot fully defend.

I used to want a clean answer, either a rule to follow or a principle that would let me stop thinking about it. I don’t trust that wish much anymore. Some questions should stay open. They should keep after you.

I still think about the pig. I don’t think the memory is asking me to stop eating meat exactly. I think it is asking me to stay awake while I do.

The Svalbard Global Seed Vault is a secure seed storage facility on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen in the Svalbard archipelago, about 1,300 kilometers from the North Pole. It opened in 2008 to store duplicate seed samples from gene banks around the world and to protect crop diversity from loss caused by war, natural disasters, equipment failure, climate change, or poor management.

The vault is built into the side of Platåberget, a sandstone mountain near Longyearbyen. Its remote Arctic location was chosen for political and environmental reasons. Svalbard is geologically stable, and its cold climate and surrounding permafrost help protect the seeds even if the power fails. The facility keeps seeds at about −18 °C (0 °F), the standard temperature for long-term seed storage.

Sometimes called the world's "doomsday vault," it works as a backup repository rather than a conventional seed bank. It does not own the seeds stored there. Under a "black box" arrangement, the seeds remain the property of the depositing institutions, and only those institutions can access them. The system supports national, regional, and international gene banks by adding another layer of security.

The vault was developed by the Government of Norway with the Nordic Genetic Resource Center (NordGen) and the Crop Trust. The Weight of Paper

After my grandmother died, I found her letters in a shoebox, bundled by year with rubber bands. Mine were there too: dutiful childhood notes about school and a lost tooth, which she had kept for decades. But it was her side of the correspondence that held me, the letters my mother had saved and eventually passed on to me.

Nothing much happens in them. The tomatoes are late. Mrs. Dolan's hip is no better. It rained Tuesday, then Wednesday, then, she wrote, “it seemed to lose interest.” I laughed out loud in my kitchen, hearing her dry voice in the slanted blue ink. She had crossed out one word and written another above it, and I could see the moment of hesitation. That small correction told me more about her than any photograph.

Maybe that is what we lose when we stop writing letters: not information, but attention. A letter shows that someone sat down and held you in mind for twenty uninterrupted minutes. They did not do it while waiting for coffee or half-watching television. They chose a page, a pen, and you. I send dozens of messages a day now, and they are quick and warm and useful, but they are also weightless. They arrive in the middle of distraction and are answered the same way. Almost none of them are kept. How could they be?

Letters also demanded a kind of patience that shaped what people said. You could not fire off a feeling and retract it ten seconds later. You had to let a thought run its course, and sometimes it changed along the way. From the shoebox I learned that my grandfather once wrote my grandmother three pages about a quarrel, and the last paragraph contradicts the first. He had not meant to forgive her when he started. The letter brought him there. A text might have kept him angry, or ended the argument in a single clipped word.

And then there was the waiting. We treat waiting now as pure cost, a flaw to engineer away. But the days between sending and receiving gave longing somewhere to live. You walked to the mailbox with a small, private hope. When something came, it had traveled to reach you. It had a stamp, a smudge, a faint smell of someone else’s house.

Last winter I wrote a letter to an old friend who had moved across the country. It took an hour and a half, much longer than I expected, because I kept finding things I had not known I wanted to say. My handwriting had gone ragged from disuse. I crossed out a word and wrote another above it. When I dropped the envelope in the box, I felt oddly exposed, as if I had handed over something I could not edit.

She wrote back three weeks later. I still have it on my desk, the paper slightly creased where her hand pressed down. It says, among other things, that it has been raining, and that the rain seems to have lost interest.

# Caching layer for the web API

## Overview
This proposal adds a caching layer to the web API to cut response times, reduce load on the database and downstream services, and handle traffic spikes more smoothly. The cache will store commonly requested responses so the API does not have to fetch the same data on every request.

## Goals
- Reduce average API response time
- Lower database and service load
- Improve throughput during traffic spikes
- Keep data freshness within acceptable bounds
- Add visibility into cache behavior

## Non-goals
- Replacing the primary database
- Caching sensitive or user-specific data without extra controls
- Keeping every endpoint perfectly fresh at all times

## Architecture
The cache will sit between the API application and its backend data sources. On each request, the API checks the cache first. If a valid entry is present, it returns that response immediately. If not, the API fetches the data from the source, returns the response, and writes it to the cache.

A distributed in-memory store such as Redis is a good fit because it offers low latency, expiration support, and mature operational tooling. For static or public GET endpoints, a CDN or edge cache could be added later.

## Cache strategy
The first version will use a cache-aside pattern:

1. The client requests a resource.
2. The API looks up the cache key.
3. If the key exists, the API returns the cached response.
4. If not, the API fetches the data from the backend.
5. The API stores the result in the cache with a TTL.
6. The API returns the response.

This pattern is straightforward and works well for read-heavy workloads.

## Key design
Cache keys should be deterministic and include:
- Endpoint path
- Normalized query parameters
- API version
- Relevant request context, such as locale

Example:
`v1:products:list:category=books:page=2:locale=en-US`

## Expiration and invalidation
Each cached item should have a TTL based on how often the underlying data changes:
- Reference data: 1–24 hours
- Frequently updated entities: 1–5 minutes
- Aggregated results: 30–120 seconds

Cache invalidation should happen when writes affect cached resources. For example, when a product changes, the system should delete or version the related product detail and listing keys. When exact invalidation is hard to manage, use shorter TTLs instead.

## Reliability considerations
To limit cache stampedes, the system should support request coalescing or a soft TTL with background refresh. Negative caching can help for known missing resources, but only for short periods. If the cache is unavailable, the API should fall back to the backend without failing the request.

## Security
Sensitive data should not be cached unless it is encrypted and scoped to a specific user. Public and shared caches should exclude authenticated or personalized responses by default.

## Observability
Track:
- Cache hit rate
- Miss rate
- Eviction rate
- Latency by endpoint
- Reduction in backend requests

Add structured logs and dashboards so the team can see whether the cache is helping and where it needs tuning.

## Rollout plan
Start with a small set of high-read, low-volatility GET endpoints. Measure hit rate and latency before and after rollout, then expand in stages. This keeps the initial scope small and gives the team a chance to validate the design in production.

The Library of Alexandria was one of the best-known libraries of the ancient world and a major center of scholarship in Alexandria, Egypt, during the Hellenistic period. It was linked to the Mouseion, or Temple of the Muses, a research institution established under the Ptolemaic dynasty after the conquests of Alexander the Great. Much about the library remains uncertain, but it has long been associated with learning and with the loss of ancient texts.

It was probably founded in the early 3rd century BCE, during the reign of Ptolemy I Soter or his son Ptolemy II Philadelphus. The Ptolemies aimed to make Alexandria a leading center of Greek culture and scholarship. They collected texts from across the Mediterranean, including works of literature, philosophy, science, mathematics, and history. Ancient sources describe aggressive acquisition practices: books brought into the city were reportedly copied, and the originals were sometimes kept for the library while copies were returned to their owners.

The library was not just a collection of scrolls. It was part of a larger scholarly community in which resident scholars studied, edited, and compared texts, helping produce critical editions of major Greek authors such as Homer. It drew prominent intellectuals, including Euclid, Eratosthenes, Aristarchus of Samothrace, and Callimachus. Callimachus is traditionally credited with compiling the Pinakes, a large bibliographic catalog often described as one of the earliest library catalogs.

Estimates of the library’s size vary widely, from tens of thousands to several hundred thousand scrolls. Its internal organization, and its relationship to a possible daughter library in the Serapeum, remain debated.

The library’s decline is well known, but it probably was not destroyed in a single event. Ancient and later sources link its decline to several episodes, including Julius Caesar’s campaign in Alexandria in 48 BCE, political unrest under Roman rule, and the destruction of pagan institutions in late antiquity, especially in the 4th century CE. Most modern historians conclude that it shrank over time rather than disappearing all at once.

Its legacy extends far beyond antiquity. The library came to stand for the idea of universal knowledge and for the vulnerability of cultural memory. In modern Alexandria, the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, opened in 2002, was conceived as a tribute to the ancient institution and its place in world history.

Ancient sources describe energetic acquisition policies: books brought into the city were reportedly copied, and in some cases the originals were kept for the library while copies were returned to their owners.

The Library of Alexandria was not merely a repository of scrolls but part of a wider scholarly community. Resident scholars studied, edited, and compared texts, helping to establish critical editions of major Greek authors such as Homer. The institution attracted prominent intellectuals, including Euclid, Eratosthenes, Aristarchus of Samothrace, and Callimachus. Callimachus is traditionally credited with compiling the Pinakes, a vast bibliographic catalogue often regarded as one of the earliest library catalogues in history.

Estimates of the library’s size vary widely, from tens of thousands to several hundred thousand scrolls. The exact organization of the library, and its relationship to a possible “daughter library” in the Serapeum, remain subjects of scholarly debate.

The destruction of the Library of Alexandria is one of the best-known episodes in cultural history, though it likely did not occur in a single catastrophic event. Ancient and later sources connect its decline to several episodes, including Julius Caesar’s campaign in Alexandria in 48 BCE, political turmoil in the Roman period, and the destruction of pagan institutions in late antiquity, especially during the 4th century CE. Modern historians generally conclude that the library diminished gradually over centuries rather than being suddenly annihilated.

The library’s legacy has lasted far beyond antiquity. It has come to represent the ideal of universal knowledge and the fragility of cultural memory. In modern Alexandria, the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, inaugurated in 2002, was conceived as a tribute to the ancient institution and its place in world history.

# Hanseatic League

The **Hanseatic League**, or **Hansa**, was a commercial and defensive network of merchant guilds and market towns in northern and central Europe. It emerged in the 12th century and was most powerful from the 13th to the 15th centuries, when it controlled much of the trade across the Baltic and North seas. Its member cities lay mainly along the coasts of what are now Germany, Poland, and the Baltic states, as well as nearby regions.

## Origins

The League grew out of associations of German merchants who traveled together for protection against piracy and banditry. The founding of Lübeck in 1143, and its rise as a gateway to the Baltic, played a central role in that process. Lübeck's alliance with Hamburg in 1241 is often treated as an early step in the League's formation. Other towns later joined, including Cologne, Bremen, Danzig (Gdańsk), Riga, and Tallinn (Reval).

## Organization

The Hansa was not a state in the modern sense. It had no standing army, permanent treasury, or formal constitution. It operated instead as a loose association whose members met in periodic assemblies called the *Hansetag*, usually held in Lübeck. Decisions were enforced through collective economic pressure, including trade embargoes, and at times through military action. Lübeck is generally considered the League's leading city and was often called its "Queen."

## Trade

Hanseatic merchants traded mainly in bulk goods. From the east they carried timber, furs, wax, amber, grain, and rye; from the west and south they brought cloth, wine, and manufactured products. Salted herring from Scania and salt from Lüneburg were also important to this trade. The League maintained major overseas trading posts, or *Kontore*, in London (the Steelyard), Bruges, Bergen, and Novgorod (the Peterhof). These settlements held special privileges and operated under their own rules.

## Conflicts

The Hansa's power brought it into conflict with rulers who opposed its trading privileges. The most important of these conflicts was its war with Denmark, which ended with the Treaty of Stralsund in 1370 and confirmed Hanseatic influence in the Baltic. Later, growing competition from Dutch, English, and Scandinavian merchants steadily weakened its position.

## Decline

From the late 15th century, the League declined for several reasons. Stronger territorial states emerged, trade routes shifted toward the Atlantic, Dutch commercial power expanded, and the member cities often failed to act together. The loss of key privileges, including the closure of the Steelyard in London in 1598, further reduced the League's influence. The last formal assembly met in 1669, although Lübeck, Hamburg, and Bremen continued to use the Hanseatic name for centuries.

## Legacy

The League left a visible mark on the cities of the Baltic region, especially in its brick Gothic architecture. Hamburg and Bremen still include "Free and Hanseatic City" in their official titles. Today, the New Hanse and the annual Hanseatic Days commemorate that history.

The Dust Bowl was a period of severe dust storms on the Great Plains in the 1930s, especially from 1934 to 1936. It grew out of a long drought, strong winds, and farming practices that left the soil exposed. The damage was environmental, economic, and social, especially in Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, Colorado, and New Mexico.

Before then, much of the Great Plains was covered in deep-rooted native grasses that held the soil in place. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, farmers plowed large areas of prairie for wheat and grazing. High crop prices and the idea that “rain follows the plow” pushed cultivation into drier, less reliable land. When drought hit in the early 1930s, the topsoil dried out and the wind carried it away.

Dust storms became the clearest sign of the disaster. Sometimes called “black blizzards,” they swept soil across farms, towns, and even distant cities. One of the best-known storms struck on April 14, 1935, a day remembered as Black Sunday, when a huge wall of dust moved across the southern Plains. The storms ruined crops, buried equipment, killed livestock, and caused breathing problems that became known as “dust pneumonia.”

The Dust Bowl made the Great Depression worse. Farm income fell, banks failed, and many families lost their land. Hundreds of thousands of people left the Plains, many heading from Oklahoma and Arkansas to California and other western states in search of work. They were often called “Okies,” though many were not from Oklahoma. Their experience later appeared in works such as John Steinbeck’s The Grapes of Wrath.

The federal government responded with conservation and relief programs under President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal. In 1935, it created the Soil Conservation Service to promote methods that reduced erosion, including contour plowing, crop rotation, strip farming, and shelterbelts of trees. Other programs helped struggling farm families stay on their land or move elsewhere.

Rain returned gradually in the late 1930s, and the worst of the crisis passed. The Dust Bowl is still remembered as one of the worst environmental disasters in U.S. history. It remains a warning about poor land use, climate extremes, and how vulnerable farming can be to ecological change.
