When I was twelve, my best friend moved across the country, and we wrote letters. They were clumsy, with crossed-out words and drawings in the margins. A reply took two weeks, sometimes three. I still remember the jolt of seeing her handwriting in the mailbox and reading each letter so many times the folds went soft. We lost touch within a year. Back then, distance could still do that.

My kids will never know that kind of loss, and I’m still not sure how I feel about it.

I notice what social media has done to friendship mostly when I try to explain it. I know what my college roommate had for dinner last night. I know her daughter lost a tooth, that her mother has been sick, that she’s unhappy at work. I haven’t spoken to her in four years. Is she still my friend? By the old definition, probably not. By the new one, she’s someone I keep up with, which feels like its own category: closeness without contact, intimacy without exchange.

There are real gifts in that. I’ve seen friendships survive moves, career changes, and the ordinary drift that used to end them. A friend in another time zone sends me voice memos while she walks her dog, and I answer while I do the dishes. It’s not the same as sitting across from her, but it’s not nothing either. It’s a thread. And threads can be tightened again. When we finally see each other, we aren’t starting from scratch.

The costs are quieter, though, and I’ve felt them more as I’ve gotten older. Social media can make friendship feel performative. I’ve caught myself framing a moment while I’m still living it, angling the dinner table for a photo, thinking of a caption while a friend is still talking. The moment becomes content, and the friend becomes, in some small way, part of the production.

It has also made affection feel cheap. A like costs nothing. A birthday message prompted by an app takes four seconds. We send these little signals and tell ourselves we’ve done the work of caring, when friendship has always asked for something slower and less convenient: showing up, sitting through the awkward silence, driving across town when someone’s life falls apart. No app has automated that, though plenty of them make it easy to pretend otherwise.

Last winter, a friend I’d known only through likes for years posted something vague and sad. I almost kept scrolling. Instead, I called her. We talked for two hours. She cried, and I realized how long it had been since I’d heard her actual voice. The post was a small flare, and I had almost treated it like part of the background.

That’s where I’ve landed. Social media didn’t ruin friendship, and it didn’t save it either. It made the circle wider and the ties looser. What we do with that is still up to us. We can treat the feed as the friendship, or we can treat it as a way back into one.

I still have my friend’s old letters, soft at the folds. I don’t want to go back to waiting three weeks for a reply. But I would like to write like that again: slowly, with crossed-out words, meaning every one.

We send these little signals and tell ourselves we’ve done the work of caring, when friendship has always asked for something slower and less convenient: showing up, sitting through the awkward silence, driving across town when someone’s life falls apart. No app has automated that, though it has made us feel as if we don’t need to.

Last winter, a friend I’d only ever "liked" from afar posted something vague and sad. I almost kept scrolling. Instead, I called her. We talked for two hours. She cried, and I realized how long it had been since I’d heard her actual voice. The post was a small flare, and I had almost treated it like part of the background.

That’s where I’ve landed. Social media didn’t ruin friendship, and it didn’t save it either. It made the circle wider and the ties looser. What we do with that is still up to us. We can treat the feed as the friendship, or we can treat it as a way back into one.

I still have my friend’s old letters, soft at the folds. I don’t want to go back to waiting three weeks for a reply. But I would like to write like that again: slowly, with crossed-out words, meaning every one.

By Thursday afternoon, the office usually feels different. People still answer emails, sit through meetings, and update spreadsheets, but the edge is gone. Conversations wander. Small tasks drag. By Friday, it can feel like everyone is acting busy more than getting much done. That is why I’ve become more open to the idea of a four-day workweek.

What persuades me is not just the appeal of an extra morning to sleep in, though that helps. It’s the fact that more time at work does not always produce better work. In many jobs, especially office jobs, productivity is not a simple count of hours. Attention runs out. Creative thinking dulls with overuse. Tired people make worse decisions. We like to talk as if stamina were the highest virtue at work, but clarity usually matters more than endurance. A shorter week accepts a basic fact: people are not machines, and treating them that way usually produces mediocre results.

I also like the idea because it treats rest as useful rather than self-indulgent. In many workplaces, exhaustion is still worn like a badge. If you are overwhelmed, you must be important; if you are unreachable, you must be needed. That logic feels thin. Rest is not the opposite of responsibility. It is part of what makes responsibility possible. An extra day away from work can mean time to recover, care for children or parents, make a doctor’s appointment without stress, read, exercise, or simply exist outside the pull of work and email. When people have room to live, they often come back more focused and less bitter.

There is also a moral case for it. For generations, new technology has been sold as a path to efficiency and freedom. For many workers, though, those gains have not meant more leisure. They have meant higher expectations. We answer messages instantly, produce documents faster, and automate routine tasks, and the reward is often just more work. A four-day workweek offers another possibility: that some of the gains from innovation could come back to people as time. Time, after all, is the resource we can never replace.

Not every profession can make the shift in the same way. Hospitals, schools, factories, and service jobs have real constraints. A four-day workweek will not solve every workplace problem. It takes careful planning, staffing changes, and a real effort not to cram five days of meetings into four. But those limits do not undercut the idea. They are a reason to rethink assumptions that no longer make much sense.

In the end, the case for a four-day workweek is a case for dignity. It asks whether work should take the best parts of our lives or support them. I don’t think people want to contribute less. I think they want to keep contributing without giving up the rest of themselves.

CEDAR FALLS, Mont. — A fast-moving wildfire burned through dry timber on the western edge of Cedar Ridge National Park on Tuesday, forcing more than 3,000 residents to evacuate and leading officials to close the park to visitors.

The fire, called the Hollow Creek Fire, was first reported shortly after 2 p.m. Monday and has burned about 14,000 acres. As of Wednesday morning, it remained 0% contained, fire officials said.

“This fire is moving faster than anything we’ve seen in this area in a decade,” Incident Commander Dana Whitfield said at an evening briefing. “Dry fuels, low humidity, and gusting winds are all working against us.”

Mandatory evacuation orders were issued for Pine Hollow, Larkspur, and parts of Cedar Falls. Another 2,000 residents in nearby areas were told to be ready to leave on short notice. Sheriff’s deputies went door to door overnight, and emergency alerts were sent to cell phones across the county.

An evacuation center opened at Cedar Falls High School, where the Red Cross provided cots, meals, and information. By midday, more than 400 people had checked in. Many arrived with pets, medication, and little else.

“We had about fifteen minutes to grab what we could,” said Maria Delgado, a Larkspur resident who left with her two children and their dog. “I took photo albums, documents, and clothes. You just hope the house is still there when you get back.”

Park Superintendent Tom Ellery said all campgrounds and trails had been cleared and that rangers had accounted for all registered backcountry visitors. “Visitor safety is our top priority,” he said. “We are also working closely with firefighters to protect historic structures, including the Ridgeline Lodge, which dates to 1932.”

More than 600 firefighters, backed by helicopters and air tankers, are fighting the fire. Crews are building containment lines near homes and working to protect power infrastructure. Two firefighters suffered minor heat-related injuries, officials said. No civilian injuries or deaths have been reported.

Smoke drifted across the region, and health officials issued air quality warnings for three counties. They urged children, older adults, and people with respiratory conditions to stay indoors.

Meteorologists said a slight chance of rain could arrive late Friday, though thunderstorms may also bring lightning and erratic winds.

Gov. Elaine Parks declared a state of emergency Tuesday, freeing additional state resources. Officials have not determined the cause of the fire, and the investigation is ongoing.

Residents can find updates and shelter information on the county emergency management website.

The first thing I noticed about my new city was how loud the silence was. In my old apartment, I knew every sound: the radiator's knock, the upstairs neighbor's heavy footsteps, the bus that groaned past at 6:40 each morning. Here, in a sublet that smelled faintly of someone else's cooking, I lay awake listening to noises I couldn't place.

Nobody tells you that moving is a kind of small, chosen amnesia. You give up your fluency. I had lived in my old city for nine years and could move through it half asleep. I knew which grocery store had the good tomatoes, which streets flooded in spring, which barista would start my order when I walked in. In the new city, I got lost on the way to the pharmacy. I stood in the cereal aisle for ten minutes, stalled by unfamiliar brands. It was humbling, and a little ridiculous, to feel like a child at thirty-four.

That humbling was also the gift. Within a week, my attention sharpened in a way it hadn't in years. I noticed the brick on my street, a warm rust that glowed at dusk. I noticed that people here nodded at strangers. I took the long way everywhere, because I didn't have a short way yet. A city you don't know forces you to look at it, and I realized that looking was a pleasure I'd let slip. Routine had sanded down my days until they felt interchangeable.

There were smaller pleasures, too. I found a bakery where the owner started saving me the end pieces of the rye loaf. I found a river path where, on Sunday mornings, runners and old men with fishing rods shared the same strip of asphalt in peaceful disregard. Each discovery felt private because nobody had pointed me to it. I had found it by wandering.

Still, the costs were real, and they arrived on their own schedule. They came on a Tuesday, when something funny happened and I reached for my phone to tell a friend, then did the time-zone math and set it back down. They came in the quiet of the second month, when the novelty wore off and I understood that friendship can't be unpacked like a box. It builds slowly, through repetition and accident, through being around. I had traded people who knew my history for people who knew only my present, and that was lonelier than I'd expected.

I've been here a year now. The bus no longer sounds foreign. I have a tomato place. Last month, a woman at the bakery asked how my week was going, and I realized I had a week worth describing. I still miss the old city, the way you miss a language you once spoke well.

I've come to think that homesickness is just the price of having loved a place, and paying it doesn't mean you made the wrong choice. Moving taught me that I could be rebuilt, that I was more portable than I'd feared. The boxes are long gone. What I carried, it turns out, was never in them.

The Dust Bowl, also called the Dirty Thirties, was a period of severe dust storms that devastated farmland across the American and Canadian prairies during the 1930s. It grew out of a long drought and years of farming that left the soil vulnerable to wind erosion. Practices such as crop rotation, cover crops, and terracing were not widely used, and once the topsoil dried out, it was easily blown away.

In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, large numbers of settlers moved onto the Great Plains, encouraged by the Homestead Acts and by an unusually wet stretch in the early 1900s. Farmers plowed up the native prairie grasses, whose deep roots had helped hold the soil in place, and planted wheat instead. High wheat prices during and after World War I pushed cultivation even further, while gasoline-powered tractors and combines made it possible to work much larger areas. Millions of acres of grassland were turned into cropland, leaving the ground exposed.

A series of droughts began in 1930 and returned in waves through 1936 and again in 1939–1940. With the grasses gone, strong winds lifted the dry topsoil into vast dust clouds. The hardest-hit area included the panhandles of Texas and Oklahoma and parts of western Kansas, eastern Colorado, and northeastern New Mexico.

On April 14, 1935, later remembered as Black Sunday, a huge storm swept dust across the southern Plains and turned day into night. The next day, journalist Robert Geiger used the term "Dust Bowl" in a news dispatch, and the name stuck. Some storms carried dust as far as Washington, D.C., and even out to ships in the Atlantic.

The storms ruined crops, buried farm equipment, and killed livestock. Many people developed "dust pneumonia" and other respiratory illnesses. Coming in the middle of the Great Depression, the disaster forced many families off their land. About 3.5 million people left the Plains states during the 1930s, many of them heading to California. Their experiences appeared in works such as John Steinbeck's The Grapes of Wrath (1939), Dorothea Lange's photographs, and Woody Guthrie's songs.

The federal government created several programs in response. The Soil Conservation Service, established in 1935 under Hugh Hammond Bennett, promoted methods such as contour plowing, strip cropping, and crop rotation. The Prairie States Forestry Project, which began in 1934, planted millions of trees in shelterbelts across the Plains. The Taylor Grazing Act of 1934 also placed grazing on public lands under federal regulation.

Rain returned in late 1939, bringing the drought to an end. The Dust Bowl remains one of the worst environmental disasters in American history, and its effects changed soil conservation policy and farming practices for decades.

The Erie Canal is a canal in New York State that shaped the country’s economy in the 19th century. It opened in 1825 and created a navigable route between the Hudson River at Albany and Lake Erie at Buffalo, linking the Atlantic coast to the Great Lakes. The canal cut transportation costs, sped up westward settlement, and helped make New York City the country’s leading port.

The idea took shape in the early 1800s, when moving people and goods across the Appalachian Mountains was slow, costly, and unreliable. Governor DeWitt Clinton became the project’s main political backer, though critics mocked it as “Clinton’s Ditch.” Construction began in 1817. Thousands of laborers, many of them immigrants, cleared forests, dug trenches, and built aqueducts and locks across difficult ground.

The original canal was about 363 miles (584 km) long, 40 feet (12 m) wide, and 4 feet (1.2 m) deep. It had 83 locks, which let boats cross more than 500 feet (150 m) of elevation change between the Hudson River and Lake Erie. The canal officially opened on October 26, 1825. Clinton marked the event with the “Wedding of the Waters,” a trip from Buffalo to New York Harbor during which water from Lake Erie was poured into the Atlantic Ocean.

The canal soon became a major transportation route in North America. Shipping costs between the Midwest and the East Coast fell sharply, making it cheaper to move crops, raw materials, and manufactured goods. Cities and towns along the route, including Syracuse, Rochester, Utica, and Buffalo, grew quickly. The canal also helped drive migration into western New York, Ohio, Indiana, and other parts of the Old Northwest.

Its success led to several enlargements during the 19th century. In the early 20th century, much of the original route became part of the larger New York State Barge Canal System, which opened in 1918 and used canalized rivers as well as new canal cuts. Railroads and highways later reduced the canal’s commercial role, but it remained an important part of the story of American engineering and expansion.

Today, the Erie Canal is used mostly for recreation, tourism, and heritage activities. It remains a well-known landmark in the history of transportation, commerce, and the growth of the United States.

The Erie Canal is a historic canal in New York State that played a major role in the economic development of the United States during the 19th century. Opened in 1825, it created a navigable water route between the Hudson River at Albany and Lake Erie at Buffalo, linking the Atlantic Ocean with the Great Lakes. The canal greatly reduced transportation costs, accelerated westward settlement, and helped establish New York City as the nation’s leading port.

At the time, overland transportation was slow, expensive, and often unreliable. Learning a second language as an adult taught me that intelligence is a smaller, humbler thing than I used to think. Before I began, I pictured language learning as a test of memory, discipline, and maybe talent. I assumed that if I worked hard enough, I would move in a straight line from confusion to fluency, picking up grammar rules and vocabulary as I went. Instead, I had to learn how to be a beginner again.

As a child, I never noticed how much of life depends on language. I moved through my first language without thinking. I joked, apologized, complained, and told stories as easily as breathing. But when I started learning another language as an adult, even simple interactions felt heavy. I could have a thought in full color and then find that I only had the words to express it in black and white. The version of me that felt quick and articulate in one language became hesitant and reduced in another. It was unsettling to realize how much of what I thought of as myself depended on speaking with ease.

That experience made me more patient, not just with myself but with other people. When you struggle to ask where the bathroom is, accidentally order the wrong food, or misunderstand a question and answer confidently anyway, you end up with a more generous view of communication. I became more aware of how much quiet courage it takes to live, work, and raise a family in a language that does not fully belong to you. Before, I admired bilingualism in the abstract. Afterward, I saw it as something lived and earned every day.

It also taught me that embarrassment does not kill you. Adults often avoid learning experiences that make them look foolish. Children do not have that option. They are corrected, misunderstood, and exposed all the time, and they keep going. Adults tend to guard competence like something breakable. Learning another language forced me to speak badly, mispronounce things, forget words I thought I knew, and hear the limits of my own mouth and memory. At first, that was frustrating. Eventually, it was freeing. I realized that improvement depends less on avoiding mistakes than on being willing to live through them.

What surprised me most was how it changed the way I listen. In my native language, I often listen for meaning alone. In a second language, I listen for structure, tone, rhythm, and intention. I pay attention to what was said, what was implied, and what I may have missed. That habit followed me back into my first language. I became slower to assume, quicker to ask, and more aware that understanding another person is never as automatic as it seems.

Learning a second language as an adult did not just give me another way to speak. It changed how I think about fluency, identity, and patience. It taught me that growth is often awkward, that humility can be useful, and that communication is both more fragile and more forgiving than I had understood. More than anything, it reminded me that becoming a beginner again is not a return to weakness. It is a return to attention.

Voters turned out in record numbers Tuesday for the Riverton School Board election, a race that usually draws far less attention than higher-profile contests.

The Riverton County Elections Office said more than 18,400 ballots were cast, or about 46 percent of registered voters in the district. Officials said it was the highest turnout for a stand-alone school-board election in the community and nearly 5,000 votes above the previous record set in 2017.

Election workers reported steady lines throughout the day, with the heaviest traffic in the morning and after work. Early voting and absentee ballots also rose sharply.

“This is the kind of civic engagement every local government hopes to see,” County Elections Director Marisol Vega said. “School-board elections typically bring in a smaller share of voters, so this level of turnout is remarkable.”

Interest in the race followed months of debate over school funding, overcrowded classrooms, campus safety, and curriculum. Candidate forums drew large audiences, and community groups on both sides ran broad outreach efforts to get residents to the polls.

Three seats were on the ballot. Incumbent Daniel Harper kept his seat, and newcomers Alicia Gomez and Trent Wallace were leading Tuesday night based on unofficial returns. Final certified results are expected later this week, but the margins appeared wide enough that the outcome was unlikely to change.

Backers of the apparent winners said the results showed voters want both continuity and change. “People care deeply about what happens in our schools,” Gomez told supporters Tuesday night. “Tonight’s turnout shows this community is paying attention and wants a voice in the decisions affecting students and families.”

Residents differed on what the results meant, but many said the turnout itself was encouraging. Parents, teachers, and retirees interviewed outside polling places said the school board affects daily life in direct ways, from academics to bus routes and extracurricular activities.

Superintendent Karen Liu said the election showed strong public interest in the district’s future.

“Regardless of who people supported, it is heartening to see so many residents participate,” Liu said. “That kind of involvement strengthens public education.”

Local analysts said the turnout could shape future elections by showing that school-board races can draw voters when the issues feel immediate and personal. For Riverton, Tuesday’s vote brought new leadership and an unusually high level of public participation.

VoltNest Energy said Tuesday it is recalling about 8,200 PowerVault S1 home batteries after receiving reports that a defect can cause the units to overheat and create a fire risk.

The PowerVault S1 is a wall-mounted battery that stores electricity from rooftop solar panels and provides backup power during outages. The recalled units were sold in the United States from March 2024 through September 2026 through solar installers and VoltNest’s website.

The company said it had received 27 overheating reports, including five cases of minor property damage such as scorched walls and melted wire insulation. It said no serious injuries had been reported, though two customers sought medical evaluation for possible smoke inhalation.

VoltNest said the problem appears to involve a manufacturing defect in lithium iron phosphate battery modules supplied by a third-party vendor. Under some charging conditions, an internal component can fail and cause excessive heat buildup.

“We are acting out of an abundance of caution,” Chief Executive Maya Levin said in a statement. “Customer safety is our top priority, and we are working closely with regulators, installers and homeowners to replace affected units as quickly as possible.”

The company told customers to shut down the battery using the main disconnect switch and not to try to repair or remove it themselves. VoltNest said it will offer free inspections, software diagnostics and replacements where needed. It also released a firmware update to reduce charging stress while replacements are arranged, but said the update does not replace the recall.

The recall was announced with the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, which told owners to follow VoltNest’s shutdown instructions and contact the company or their installer. The agency said affected units have serial numbers beginning with PVS1-24 and PVS1-25.

The recall is an early challenge for VoltNest, a venture-backed company founded in 2021 that has expanded with demand for home backup power during outages and extreme weather.

“Recalls are damaging, especially for a young brand,” energy storage analyst Daniel Cho said. “But in this industry, transparency and speed matter. Homeowners need confidence that these systems are safe inside their garages and utility rooms.”

# Svalbard Global Seed Vault

The **Svalbard Global Seed Vault** (Norwegian: *Svalbard globale frøhvelv*) is a secure backup facility for crop diversity on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen in the Svalbard archipelago. Media reports often call it the "Doomsday Vault." It stores duplicate seed samples from gene banks around the world to protect collections from loss through accident, mismanagement, war, or natural disaster.

## History

The idea for the vault was proposed in the 1980s and later advanced through the work of agricultural scientist Cary Fowler, who went on to lead the Global Crop Diversity Trust, now the Crop Trust. The Norwegian government paid for construction, which cost about NOK 50 million. The facility opened on 26 February 2008.

## Location and design

The vault is built into a sandstone mountain near Longyearbyen, about 1,300 kilometres from the North Pole, and stands roughly 130 metres above sea level. The site was chosen in part to place it above projected sea-level rise. A tunnel about 120 metres long leads to three storage chambers, each built to hold up to 1.5 million seed samples. Total capacity is 4.5 million varieties, or about 2.25 billion seeds.

The vault has become a symbol of international cooperation on food security and biodiversity conservation. The 2017 flooding also showed that climate change can affect even facilities designed for long-term protection.

I have never trusted any habit that arrives with too much ceremony. The ones that save me are usually smaller: making coffee before I am fully awake, opening a window even in winter, walking for no particular reason. Of these, walking is the one I rely on most. It asks the least of me and gives back the most.

I did not always think of walking as a practice. For a long time, it was just what happened between places. It belonged to errands, late buses, parking two streets away, crossing campus in bad weather. It was practical, forgettable, and sometimes a little annoying. Somewhere along the way, though, it changed categories. It stopped feeling like a delay before life and became a way of entering it.

Part of its comfort is how plain it is. Walking does not require talent, special equipment, or the right mood. It does not ask me to improve myself. On days when I am tired, restless, or vaguely discontented in the modern way, too much screen, too many tabs open in my mind, I can still put on shoes and go outside. That simplicity feels corrective. So much of life now is frictionless in the wrong ways: messages arrive instantly, news follows me from room to room, entire afternoons disappear while my body stays still. Walking brings back a useful kind of friction. It reminds me that distance is real, weather is real, my legs are real.

I have noticed that my thoughts behave differently when I walk. At a desk, problems often harden. They take on the dense, airless quality of something overhandled. But on a walk, even familiar worries begin to loosen. The rhythm of steps gives the mind just enough to do that it stops gripping so tightly. I have had ideas arrive while crossing intersections, remembered lines I thought were lost, forgiven people a little, forgiven myself a little. None of this feels mystical. Movement just changes the scale of thought. What seems inescapable indoors becomes, outside, one thing among many: a barking dog, a passing train, the smell of cut grass, the sudden authority of a tree.

Walking also returns me to my senses in the most literal way. I start to notice the world not as backdrop but as company. The same street is never exactly the same street. There are seasonal revisions: wet leaves plastered to the sidewalk, the medicinal brightness of cold air, the tired abundance of late-summer gardens. There are small neighborhood dramas too: a child chalking suns on the pavement, someone learning to ride a bicycle, a curtain lifted and dropped. To walk regularly is to become a modest witness. You learn the habits of dogs, the timing of sprinklers, where the first crocuses insist on appearing. Familiarity accumulates, and with it a quiet affection.

What I value most, though, is that walking offers a kind of progress that cannot be optimized into meaninglessness. One foot in front of the other is both an instruction and a philosophy. You do not have to leap. You do not have to finish everything today. You move, you pause, you continue. There is humility in that, and relief.

When I come back from a walk, my life is usually unchanged in any measurable sense. The emails are still there, and so are the unanswered questions. But I feel slightly rejoined to myself. I have been reminded that the world extends beyond my preoccupations and that I can meet it with my own body, at a human pace. For such an ordinary habit, walking has a rare power: it brings me back to proportion. More and more, that feels like a form of grace.

## Create calendar event

Creates a new event on a user's calendar.

### Endpoint

`POST /v1/events`

### Description

Creates a calendar event with a title, start time, and end time. You can also include a description, location, attendees, reminders, recurrence, and time zone.

If the request succeeds, the API returns the new event object, including its unique ID.

### Authentication

Send a valid bearer token in the `Authorization` header:

```http
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
```

### Request headers

| Header | Type | Required | Description |
|--------|------|----------|-------------|
| Authorization | string | Yes | Bearer access token |
| Content-Type | string | Yes | Must be `application/json` |

### Request body

```json
{
  "title": "Team Sync",
  "start": "2026-11-20T09:00:00Z",
  "end": "2026-11-20T09:30:00Z",
  "description": "Weekly project status meeting",
  "location": "Conference Room A",
  "timezone": "UTC",
  "attendees": [
    "alex@example.com",
    "sam@example.com"
  ],
  "reminders": [
    {
      "method": "email",
      "minutesBefore": 30
    }
  ],
  "recurrence": {
    "frequency": "weekly",
    "interval": 1
  }
}
```

### Body parameters

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|------|------|----------|-------------|
| title | string | Yes | Event title. Maximum 200 characters. |
| start | string | Yes | Start date and time in ISO 8601 format |
| end | string | Yes | End date and time in ISO 8601 format |
| description | string | No | Event details. Maximum 5000 characters. |
| location | string | No | Event location |
| timezone | string | No | IANA time zone, for example `America/New_York` |
| attendees | array[string] | No | List of attendee email addresses |
| reminders | array[object] | No | Reminder settings |
| reminders[].method | string | Yes | `email` or `popup` |
| reminders[].minutesBefore | integer | Yes | Number of minutes before the event starts |
| recurrence | object | No | Recurrence settings |
| recurrence.frequency | string | No | `daily`, `weekly`, `monthly`, or `yearly` |
| recurrence.interval | integer | No | Repeat interval. Must be greater than 0. |

### Response

**201 Created**

```json
{
  "id": "evt_01J9X8K7M2R4A6P9",
  "title": "Team Sync",
  "start": "2026-11-20T09:00:00Z",
  "end": "2026-11-20T09:30:00Z",
  "description": "Weekly project status meeting",
  "location": "Conference Room A",
  "timezone": "UTC",
  "attendees": [
    "alex@example.com",
    "sam@example.com"
  ],
  "status": "confirmed",
  "createdAt": "2026-11-10T14:22:31Z"
}
```

### Error responses

| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| 400 Bad Request | Missing required fields, invalid JSON, or malformed dates |
| 401 Unauthorized | Missing or invalid access token |
| 403 Forbidden | Token does not have permission to create events |
| 409 Conflict | Event overlaps with a protected calendar block |
| 422 Unprocessable Entity | Validation failed, such as `end` occurring before `start` |

Example error:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "validation_error",
    "message": "The `end` time must be later than `start`."
  }
}
```

### Notes

- Use ISO 8601 format for all timestamps.
- If you omit `timezone`, the calendar's default time zone is used.
- Depending on account settings, attendees may receive invitations.
- A recurring event may create a series instead of a single event.

Riverbend Health said Tuesday that hackers may have stolen the personal and medical information of about 378,000 current and former patients.

The Ohio-based network, which operates seven hospitals and more than 40 outpatient clinics, said it discovered suspicious activity on March 4 after IT staff noticed unusual data transfers from a server used for billing records. Investigators believe the attackers may have been in the system since mid-February.

"We regret this incident and the concern it causes our patients," said Dr. Elaine Marchetti, Riverbend Health's chief executive. "We are working to understand what happened and to reduce the risk of it happening again."

Riverbend said the exposed data may include names, birth dates, home addresses, Social Security numbers, insurance information, and details about diagnoses and treatment. The network said it found no evidence that the attackers reached its electronic health record system, which stores full clinical charts, but said the investigation is still underway.

Emergency departments stayed open, but some scheduling and billing systems were offline for nearly a week. Several patients said appointments were rescheduled and test results were delayed.

"I showed up for a follow-up and they were writing everything on paper," said Dana Whitfield, 54, who receives care at a Riverbend cardiology clinic. "Now I'm worried about who has my information."

Riverbend said it hired an outside cybersecurity firm and notified the FBI and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, which keeps a public list of major health care breaches. The network said it has not received a ransom demand, though a ransomware group has claimed responsibility on a dark web leak site and posted what it says are sample files. Riverbend said it is reviewing that claim.

Health care organizations remain frequent targets for cyberattacks because medical records can be used for identity theft and fraud, said Raymond Okafor, a health care cybersecurity consultant not involved in the investigation.

"A stolen credit card can be canceled in minutes," Okafor said. "A Social Security number and medical history can be exploited for years."

Riverbend said it will begin mailing notification letters next week and will offer two years of free credit monitoring and identity theft protection. Patients can call a dedicated hotline at 1-800-555-0142.

The network advised patients to review insurance statements for unfamiliar charges and consider placing fraud alerts on their credit files.

*RIVERBEND, Ohio* — Riverbend Health, a regional network of seven hospitals and more than 40 outpatient clinics, confirmed Tuesday that attackers gained unauthorized access to its systems and may have stolen personal and medical information belonging to approximately 378,000 current and former patients.

In a statement posted to its website, the network said it discovered suspicious activity on March 4 after IT staff noticed unusual data transfers from a server used to store billing records. The network said the intruders appear to have had access since mid-February.

"We deeply regret this incident and the concern it causes our patients," said Dr. Elaine Marchetti, Riverbend Health's chief executive. "Protecting patient information is central to our mission, and we are taking every step to understand what happened and prevent it from happening again."

According to the network, the compromised data may include names, birth dates, home addresses, Social Security numbers, insurance information, and details of diagnoses and treatments. Riverbend said it found no evidence that the attackers accessed its electronic health record system, which holds full clinical charts, though the investigation is ongoing.

Emergency departments remained open during the incident, but the network confirmed that some scheduling and billing systems were taken offline for nearly a week. Several patients reported rescheduled appointments and delayed test results.

"I showed up for a follow-up and they were writing everything on paper," said Dana Whitfield, 54, who receives care at a Riverbend cardiology clinic. "Now I'm worried about who has my information."

The network said it has not received a ransom demand, though a ransomware group has claimed responsibility on a dark web leak site and posted what it says are sample files. # Antikythera mechanism

The **Antikythera mechanism** is an ancient Greek hand-powered orrery and is often described as the earliest known analog computer. It was used to predict astronomical positions and eclipses years in advance and to track cycles in the Greek calendar, including the dates of major Panhellenic games. The device is generally dated to the 2nd or 1st century BCE.

## Discovery

The mechanism was recovered in 1901 from a Roman-era shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera, between Kythera and Crete. Sponge divers found the wreck in 1900, and salvage operations led by the Greek Navy and archaeologists brought up statues, pottery, jewelry, coins, and a corroded lump of bronze. That lump was later found to contain gears and inscriptions. The mechanism is now held at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

## Construction

The device was enclosed in a wooden case about the size of a shoebox. Its bronze parts, many thin and finely cut, survive in 82 known fragments. Turning a crank drove a system of at least 30 interlocking gears with triangular teeth, which moved pointers across dials on the front and back of the case.

The front dial showed the positions of the Sun and Moon in the zodiac along with a calendar. The Moon's phase appeared on a small rotating, partly silvered ball. The back had two large spiral dials: one for the Metonic cycle, which spans 19 years and reconciles solar years with lunar months, and one for the Saros cycle, about 18 years long and used to predict eclipses. Smaller subsidiary dials tracked other cycles, including the Callippic cycle and the Olympiad cycle.

The Moon's irregular motion, caused by its elliptical orbit, was modeled with a pin-and-slot mechanism that used two gears with offset axes. This matches the lunar theory attributed to Hipparchus.

## Research

Early studies by Valerios Stais, and later by Derek de Solla Price in the 1950s through 1970s, established its basic function. X-ray imaging in the 1970s and the Antikythera Mechanism Research Project, which began in 2005, used microfocus X-ray computed tomography and surface imaging to read much of the inscriptions, which amount to a user's manual. Researchers have also proposed that the device displayed planetary positions, and reconstructions of such gearing have been published, though the evidence is still incomplete.

## Significance

The mechanism's complexity has no known parallel among surviving artifacts for more than a thousand years, until medieval astronomical clocks in Europe and the Islamic world. Its origin is still debated, with possible links to Rhodes, Corinth, or Syracuse, and to the traditions of Hipparchus or Archimedes. It remains one of the clearest surviving examples of Hellenistic technology and astronomical knowledge.

# Photo Date Renamer

A command-line tool that renames photo files using the date they were taken, read from EXIF metadata. It helps keep photo libraries organized across folders and devices.

## Features

- Renames photos using the original capture date from EXIF metadata
- Supports JPG and JPEG files
- Uses consistent, sortable filenames
- Adds a counter when multiple files share the same timestamp
- Can process one folder or scan subfolders recursively
- Includes a dry-run mode so you can preview changes before renaming anything

## Why use it?

Cameras and phones often produce filenames like `IMG_4032.JPG` or `DSC00123.jpg`. Those names stop being useful once the files are mixed into a larger collection. This tool replaces them with timestamp-based names such as:

```bash
2023-08-14_18-42-09.jpg
2023-08-14_18-42-09_2.jpg
```

The result is easier to read, sort, and manage, especially when you merge photos from different devices.

## Installation

Clone the repository and install the dependencies:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/yourname/photo-date-renamer.git
cd photo-date-renamer
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

If the package is published, you may also be able to install it with:

```bash
pip install photo-date-renamer
```

## Usage

Rename all supported photos in a folder:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos
```

Process folders recursively:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos --recursive
```

Preview changes without modifying files:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos --dry-run
```

Specify a custom filename format:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos --format "%Y/%m/%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S"
```

## Filename behavior

By default, files are renamed with this pattern:

```text
YYYY-MM-DD_HH-MM-SS.ext
```

Examples:

- `IMG_0001.JPG` → `2022-05-06_14-33-21.jpg`
- `DSC7788.jpeg` → `2022-05-06_14-33-21_2.jpeg`

If two or more photos have the same timestamp, the tool adds a numeric suffix to avoid collisions.

## Missing metadata

If a file does not contain a valid capture date in its EXIF metadata, the tool skips it and reports that in the summary output. A future version may optionally fall back to the file's creation or modification time.

## Safety

- Does not overwrite existing files without warning
- Supports dry runs for previewing changes safely
- Reports renamed, skipped, and failed files at the end

## Example output

```bash
Renamed: IMG_1203.JPG -> 2021-11-03_09-15-44.jpg
Renamed: IMG_1204.JPG -> 2021-11-03_09-15-45.jpg
Skipped: scan_01.jpg (no EXIF date found)

Done. 2 renamed, 1 skipped, 0 failed.
```

## Contributing

Issues and pull requests are welcome. If you find a bug or want to suggest a feature, open an issue with sample filenames, expected behavior, and your platform details.

## License

MIT License.

Wildfire Forces Evacuations Near Redwood Canyon National Park

REDWOOD COUNTY, Calif. — A fast-moving wildfire near Redwood Canyon National Park prompted mandatory evacuations Tuesday as firefighters contended with dry vegetation, gusty winds and steep terrain.

The Canyon Ridge Fire started late Monday afternoon about five miles east of the park’s southern boundary and had burned an estimated 7,800 acres by Tuesday evening, according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection. Containment was still low as crews worked to protect homes, campgrounds and infrastructure in nearby mountain communities.

Evacuation orders covered the towns of Pine Creek, Alder Grove and Millstone, along with several rural neighborhoods near Highway 86. Officials also issued warnings for parts of the park’s gateway communities and told visitors to be ready to leave on short notice.

“This fire is moving rapidly and conditions can change minute by minute,” Incident Commander Laura Mendes said at an evening briefing. “Our top priority is life safety, getting people out of harm’s way and giving firefighters the room they need to work.”

No deaths or serious injuries had been reported by Tuesday night, though officials said several structures were at risk and at least two outbuildings had burned. The cause remained under investigation.

Part of Highway 86 was closed to non-emergency traffic, and park officials temporarily shut the park’s southern entrance, several backcountry trails and campgrounds. Rangers began escorting campers out of affected areas early Tuesday as smoke settled into nearby valleys and reduced visibility across the region.

The National Weather Service issued a red flag warning for the area, citing low humidity, high temperatures and wind gusts that could top 30 mph. Fire officials said those conditions were expected to continue into Wednesday, making containment more difficult.

More than 600 firefighters, backed by air tankers, helicopters and bulldozers, were assigned to the fire. Crews worked overnight to cut containment lines and protect structures in evacuation zones.

At an evacuation center at Redwood County High School, residents arrived with pets, medications and a few belongings. Volunteers distributed food, water and blankets as families waited for updates.

“We grabbed what we could and left,” Pine Creek resident Maria Lopez said. “You could see the glow on the ridge, and the wind was just pushing it closer.”

Officials urged residents to follow emergency alerts and stay away from the area. “If you have been told to leave, leave now,” Mendes said. “Do not wait to see the fire.”

# Commit message style guide

A good commit message says what changed and why. Future readers should be able to understand the history without reading every diff.

Keep messages clear, consistent, and concise.

## Structure

Use this format:

```text
<type>: <short summary>

<optional body>

<optional footer>
```

### 1. Short summary

- Keep it to 50 characters or fewer when possible.
- Use the imperative mood: “add,” “fix,” “remove,” not “added” or “fixes.”
- Start with a lowercase type followed by a colon.
- Do not end the summary with a period.

Examples:

- `fix: handle null response in user service`
- `docs: clarify local setup steps`
- `refactor: simplify cache invalidation logic`

### 2. Body

Add a body when the summary does not tell the whole story.

Guidelines:

- Wrap lines at about 72 characters.
- Explain why the change was made before describing the implementation.
- Include context, tradeoffs, side effects, or migration notes when relevant.
- Use short paragraphs or bullet points.

A useful checklist:

- What problem existed?
- Why choose this approach?
- Are there risks or follow-up tasks?

### 3. Footer

Use footers for metadata when needed:

- Issue references: `Refs: #123`
- Closing references: `Closes: #456`
- Breaking changes: `BREAKING CHANGE: config format has changed`

## Recommended types

Use a small, predictable set of types. Common choices:

- `feat`: new functionality
- `fix`: bug fix
- `docs`: documentation only
- `refactor`: code change without behavior change
- `test`: tests added or updated
- `chore`: maintenance, tooling, or dependency updates
- `perf`: performance improvement
- `build`: build system or dependency management changes
- `ci`: continuous integration changes

## Best practices

- Keep each commit to one logical change.
- Write the message like a command:
  - “add validation for empty emails”
  - “remove deprecated API client”
- Be specific. Prefer:
  - `fix: prevent duplicate invoice creation`
  instead of:
  - `fix: bug fixes`
- If a commit is large or complex, explain it.
- Review the message before committing. It becomes part of the project history.

## Avoid

- Vague summaries like `update stuff` or `misc fixes`
- Long subject lines
- Describing only the code, not the reason
- Combining unrelated changes in one commit
- Auto-generated messages left unedited, such as `WIP` or `temp`

## Example

```text
fix: prevent retry loop on expired auth token

The client kept retrying requests after receiving a 401 response,
which caused unnecessary traffic and delayed user-facing errors.

Stop retries when the token is expired and show a re-auth
prompt instead.

Closes: #214
```

Consistency matters more than perfection. A simple shared standard makes project history easier to read, search, and maintain.

## Installation

This library requires Python 3.8 or later and is available as a standard Python package.

Install it with `pip`:

```bash
pip install csvparser
```

If you're working in a project, you may want to create a virtual environment first:

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate      # macOS / Linux
.venv\Scripts\activate         # Windows
pip install csvparser
```

To check that the installation worked:

```bash
python -c "import csvparser; print(csvparser.__version__)"
```

To install from source, clone the repository and use editable mode:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/your-org/csvparser.git
cd csvparser
pip install -e .
```

In editable mode, local code changes are available immediately without reinstalling the package.

---

## Quick Start

Use `CSVParser` to read a CSV file as rows of dictionaries.

Given a file named `people.csv`:

```csv
name,age,city
Alice,30,London
Bob,25,Paris
Charlie,35,Berlin
```

You can parse it like this:

```python
from csvparser import CSVParser

parser = CSVParser("people.csv")
rows = parser.read()

for row in rows:
    print(row)
```

Output:

```python
{'name': 'Alice', 'age': '30', 'city': 'London'}
{'name': 'Bob', 'age': '25', 'city': 'Paris'}
{'name': 'Charlie', 'age': '35', 'city': 'Berlin'}
```

### Reading rows one at a time

The Fifth Day

For six years, Sunday evenings came with a low hum of dread. Nothing was exactly wrong. The job was fine. My colleagues were kind. But the weekend kept slipping away. Saturday went to errands and recovery; Sunday to thinking about Monday. I was living around my life instead of in it.

Then my company tried a four-day week: same pay, same expectations. I assumed there had to be a catch. Either we'd end up working ten-hour days, or Friday's work would pile up and wait for us on Monday.

What happened was simpler and stranger than that. The work compressed. Meetings that used to drift for an hour got to the point in twenty minutes. We stopped holding meetings to plan other meetings. With only four days, people guarded their time. They said no more often, and the important things still got done.

Later, I found the research matched what I had felt. In the 2022 UK pilot, involving about 61 companies and roughly 2,900 workers, most firms kept the shorter week afterward. Workers reported less burnout and better sleep, and revenue stayed about the same. Earlier trials in Iceland found much the same. That does not mean every workplace can do this. It does challenge the idea that more hours automatically create more value.

That idea comes from an older model of work. The five-day week made sense in an industrial economy, when output tracked time on a factory floor. Much of today's work does not work that way. Knowledge work depends on attention, and attention does not increase in a straight line with hours. For me, the fifth day was often the one spent half-present, answering emails mostly to show I was there.

What I got back was not only rest, though rest mattered. I got ordinary life back. I could go to the dentist without performing calendar acrobatics. I could cook an actual dinner on a Friday. I spent a long afternoon with my father, who is older now, and noticed how much of our relationship had been squeezed into scraps of leftover time. A day off is not really a luxury. It is where the rest of life fits.

The objections are real. A four-day week is harder to arrange for nurses, teachers, and restaurant staff, whose work cannot be reshaped just by cutting meetings. But that is an argument for careful design, not for giving up where it could work. It means staggered shifts, more hiring, and honest measurement. And it means resisting the fake version of the idea, where five days of work are simply crammed into four longer ones. The point is not fewer days at the same cost to a person. The point is fewer hours, used better.

I don't think a four-day week fixes everything. Bad managers will still be bad. Pressure will still find new places to settle. But I came out of that pilot clearer about what work is for. It is part of a life. It is not the structure that everything else has to fit inside.

These days, Sunday evenings are quiet. I notice that more than any productivity statistic.

In seventh grade, I had a math teacher named Mr. Okafor who did something that drove me crazy at the time: he wouldn't give me the answer.

I was stuck on a word problem about two trains, so I raised my hand, sure that adults were supposed to clear up confusion on demand. He came over, looked at my paper, and asked, "What do you know so far?" I told him nothing. He said, "Great. Let's write that down." Then he waited. Not impatiently, not with a sigh, just quietly, as if there were no reason to rush. After a while, mostly to break the silence, I started listing what I did know: the trains left at different times, one was faster. Halfway through saying it, I saw the answer.

I've remembered that moment for years. It taught me that teaching isn't just about giving someone information. It's about helping them become the kind of person who can work things out.

Knowing the material still matters, of course. A teacher who doesn't understand the subject can't help much. But I've known brilliant people who were awful teachers because they had forgotten what it felt like to be lost. Expertise can make a person short with confusion. Mr. Okafor treated confusion as normal. He never made me feel dumb for not knowing.

That's the second part, I think: a good teacher makes it safe to be wrong. In his class, mistakes went on the board for everyone to look at, not to embarrass anyone, but to figure out what happened. "Interesting," he'd say. "Where did this go sideways?" We learned to trace our mistakes instead of hiding them. I've carried that into adult life, where admitting an error early can keep a small problem from turning into a disaster.

The third part is harder to pin down. Good teachers believe in you a little before you've done anything to deserve it. Once, Mr. Okafor handed me a problem from a competition packet meant for older students and said, "I think you'd enjoy this one." I couldn't solve it. Still, I spent a week trying, and I remember what it felt like to be taken seriously. His confidence in me came first. I worked to catch up to it.

Since then, I've had teachers who were more charismatic, more entertaining, more widely admired. Some of them were excellent. But when I think about who changed the way I think, I come back to the man standing beside my desk, letting the silence last until I filled it.

Teaching like that takes restraint. It would have been quicker for him to show me the solution, and I probably would have felt grateful for ten minutes. Instead, he gave me something that lasted longer: the feeling of figuring it out for myself, and the realization that I could.

I don't remember the answer to the train problem. I remember the silence. I think that's the point.

# Regional Airline Cancels Dozens of Flights as Pilot Shortage Deepens

**Skyline Air grounds routes to smaller cities, leaving thousands of travelers scrambling**

*By Staff Reporter*

Regional carrier Skyline Air said Monday that it will cancel about 120 flights over the next six weeks because it does not have enough qualified pilots.

The cuts will affect service to eight mid-sized and rural markets, including Cedar Falls, Marlow County, and Pine Harbor. Three of those communities will lose daily service entirely until at least mid-March, according to a company statement.

"We regret the disruption to our customers and the communities we serve," said Dana Whitfield, Skyline Air's chief operating officer. "We have exhausted every option to cover these routes safely and within federal duty-time regulations. Without enough pilots, we cannot operate the schedule we promised."

The airline said it has lost nearly 15 percent of its pilot workforce over the past year as many left for major carriers offering higher pay, signing bonuses, and faster routes to international flying. Skyline now employs about 340 pilots, down from 400 last January.

Analysts said Skyline's troubles reflect a broader national shortage. A wave of retirements among veteran pilots, along with a federal requirement that airline captains log 1,500 flight hours, has narrowed the pipeline of new hires. Regional airlines, which often serve as a stepping stone to major carriers, have been hit especially hard.

"Regionals are the farm system of the industry," said Marcus Tran, an aviation consultant. "When the big airlines hire aggressively, the regionals lose talent. Then the small towns that depend on them lose air service, and it's very hard to get it back."

For passengers, the effects were immediate. At Cedar Falls Regional Airport on Monday, traveler Priya Natarajan said her flight to a family wedding was canceled with two days' notice.

"I got a text and an email, and that was it," she said. "Now I'm looking at a five-hour drive to the nearest hub."

Local officials said they were worried about longer-term effects. Cedar Falls Mayor Tom Hendricks said reliable air service is important for attracting employers and supporting local businesses.

"Losing flights isn't just an inconvenience," he said. "It affects our economy."

Skyline said affected passengers will receive full refunds or be rebooked on partner airlines where possible. The company also announced a new retention package, including raises of up to 18 percent and a tuition-assistance program for aspiring pilots.

Whitfield said the airline hopes to restore full service by April but did not guarantee a timeline.

## Public bike-share service FAQ

### 1. What is the bike-share service?
The bike-share service lets you rent a bike for short trips around the city. You can pick up a bike at one station and return it to any station in the network with an open dock.

### 2. How do I sign up?
Sign up in the app or on the website. Create an account, choose a pass or membership, and add a payment method. Once you're registered, you can unlock bikes in the app.

### 3. What types of passes are available?
We offer single rides, day passes, and monthly or annual memberships. Short-term passes work well for visitors. Memberships make more sense for regular riders. For current prices, check the website or app.

### 4. How do I unlock a bike?
Open the app, find a nearby station or bike, and scan the QR code or enter the bike number. The lock will open automatically. If that doesn't work, contact customer support.

### 5. Where can I return a bike?
Return bikes to any official bike-share station with an open dock. Make sure the bike locks into place, then wait for confirmation in the app so you aren't charged for extra time.

### 6. Is there a time limit for rides?
Yes. The time limit depends on the pass or membership you bought. If you go over the included ride time, extra fees may apply. You can check your ride details in the app at any time.

### 7. What if a station is full?
If your destination station is full, check the app for nearby stations with open docks. Depending on your plan, you may get a short grace period to return the bike at the next station.

### 8. What should I do if a bike is damaged?
If you spot a problem before or during your ride, report it in the app right away and take another bike if you can. That helps us keep the fleet safe and working properly.

### 9. Do I need to wear a helmet?
We strongly recommend wearing a helmet. Local law may require one for certain age groups, so check the rules in your area before you ride.

### 10. What happens if a bike is lost or stolen?
If a bike is lost or stolen during your rental, contact customer support right away. File a police report if required. Charges may continue until the bike is recovered or the case is resolved.

### 11. How can I contact customer support?
You can reach customer support through the app, the website, or by phone. For current contact details and service hours, see the Help section.

I grew up in a family where meat was as ordinary as the table it was served on. We had roast chicken on Sundays, bacon on weekends, burgers in summer. No one talked about the ethics of eating animals because it did not seem like an ethical question. Meat was food. Food kept the family fed and brought us to the table. If we felt gratitude, it was for the person who cooked, not for the animal that had died.

My view changed gradually, not all at once. I remember standing in a grocery store, looking at cuts of meat wrapped in plastic, and feeling for the first time how far the product had been separated from the life it came from. The packaging did more than preserve the meat; it kept the thought at a distance. Once I started noticing that distance, I could not stop. I saw that my appetite depended on not looking too closely. I liked animals in theory, but when they became dinner, I preferred not to think about them at all.

That, to me, is where the ethical problem starts. Most people would agree that animal suffering matters. We can recognize pain in a dog, fear in a cow, distress in a chicken. Yet the food system often treats animals as products rather than living creatures with lives of their own. If causing unnecessary suffering is wrong, then industrial meat production is hard to defend. The confinement, mutilation, and slaughter happen on such a scale that it can feel unreal. That may be part of why the system endures. It is easier to take part in something cruel when the cruelty is buried under routine and convenience.

At the same time, I do not want to turn the question into a test of personal purity. Eating meat is bound up with culture, class, geography, and memory. For some people it is tradition; for others it is survival, health, or the limits of what they can afford and access. It makes no sense to pretend everyone chooses from the same set of options. Someone buying cheap meat to feed a family under financial strain is not making the same choice as someone eating animal products as a luxury. Moral judgment without social context can slip into self-congratulation.

Even so, complexity is not a reason to stop caring. The fact that no one can live perfectly does not mean we are free from trying. I do not have a pure or final answer. I eat less meat than I used to, and when I do eat it, I feel that choice more clearly. For me, the ethics of eating meat is not only about whether killing animals can ever be justified. It is also about whether I am willing to let comfort keep me from paying attention. If ethical eating is possible at all, it starts there: looking plainly at what feeds us, what it costs, and who bears that cost.

At thirty-four, I stood in a Lisbon bakery trying to remember a sentence. I wanted a coffee and a custard tart. I’d practiced on the walk over, but when the woman behind the counter looked up, the words vanished. I pointed and said “this” twice. She smiled kindly, the way you smile at a child, and I felt my face burn.

That was the first thing Portuguese taught me: how much of my adult identity depended on sounding competent. At home, I was someone people asked for help. In that bakery, I had the vocabulary of a toddler and the pride of a department head, and the two did not mix.

For months, I was a reduced version of myself. I couldn’t joke, argue, or make the offhand comment that gives a person shape. My personality, which I’d thought of as fixed, turned out to lean heavily on grammar. What came through instead was simpler: patient, a little earnest, often confused. Strangely, people liked that person. My neighbor, Dona Fernanda, who was seventy and had never left Portugal, started correcting me with great ceremony. “Not eu sou cansado,” she’d say. “Estou cansado. You are tired, but you are not made of tired.” I’ve never forgotten the difference between permanent and temporary states, and I think about it in English now too.

The second lesson was about listening. In my first language, I listened carelessly, already drafting my reply. In Portuguese, I had to catch each word as it came. I started noticing tone, gesture, and the pauses people left for each other. I became a better listener in both languages, and I was a little ashamed of how much I’d missed before.

The third lesson was that mistakes don’t kill you. Once, at a dinner table, I told everyone I was “very constipated” when I meant embarrassed. The words are false friends, and that is all I’ll say about it. The table erupted, someone topped up my glass, and I felt more included than I had all week. Failing in public, I learned, mostly makes people kinder. I had spent years avoiding the very thing that might have made me relax.

Progress was invisible until it wasn’t. For a long time, I felt stuck. Then one afternoon I realized I’d followed an entire conversation between two fast-talking taxi drivers and laughed at the right moment. No one handed me a certificate. A door I hadn’t known was shut was suddenly open.

I still make mistakes every day, and I still notice the slight gentleness people use with foreigners. But I don’t hear it as pity anymore. I hear it as hospitality, offered to anyone willing to stand in front of strangers and be bad at something.

What I carry from those years is not fluency exactly. It’s a willingness to be the smaller person, to point and say “this” and try again. That person, it turns out, was never lesser. He was just learning, which was the one thing I had stopped letting myself do.

# Erie Canal

The Erie Canal is a canal in the U.S. state of New York that connects the Hudson River at Albany with Lake Erie at Buffalo. Completed in 1825, it was the first navigable waterway linking the Atlantic coast to the Great Lakes and helped drive economic growth in the United States during the nineteenth century.

## History

Plans for a canal across upstate New York circulated in the late eighteenth century. The project moved forward under Governor DeWitt Clinton, who secured state funding in 1817 after federal support failed. Critics called it "Clinton's Ditch." Construction began on July 4, 1817, in Rome, New York.

The canal was built largely by hand. Laborers, many of them Irish immigrants, worked with horses, oxen, and simple tools. Engineers with little formal training, including Benjamin Wright and James Geddes, developed methods for clearing forests, removing stumps, and cutting through swampland. The original canal was about 363 miles (584 km) long, 40 feet (12 m) wide, and 4 feet (1.2 m) deep. It had 83 locks and overcame an elevation change of about 565 feet (172 m).

The canal officially opened on October 26, 1825. Clinton traveled from Buffalo to New York City in a ceremonial voyage and poured Lake Erie water into the Atlantic Ocean in what became known as the "Wedding of the Waters."

## Economic and social impact

The canal cut both shipping costs and travel time. The cost of moving a ton of goods from Buffalo to New York City fell from about $100 to about $10, and trips that had taken weeks could be completed in days. Farm products from the Midwest moved east, while manufactured goods and settlers moved west.

New York City overtook ports such as Philadelphia and Boston and became the country's leading commercial center. Cities along the route, including Syracuse, Rochester, Utica, and Buffalo, grew quickly. The canal corridor also became associated with religious revivals, the women's rights movement, and abolitionism. Because of this activity, some historians have called western New York the "burned-over district."

## Enlargement and modern use

The canal was enlarged between 1836 and 1862. From 1905 to 1918 it was replaced by the larger New York State Barge Canal, which used rivers and lakes as parts of its route. Railroads, highways, and the St. Lawrence Seaway reduced commercial traffic in the twentieth century.

Today the canal is used mainly for recreation, including boating, cycling, and tourism along the Erie Canalway Trail. In 2000, Congress designated the Erie Canalway National Heritage Corridor to help preserve it. The canal is operated by the New York State Canal Corporation.

Proposals for a canal across upstate New York circulated in the late eighteenth century, but the project gained momentum under the advocacy of Governor DeWitt Clinton, who secured state funding in 1817 after federal support failed to materialize. The venture was derided as "Clinton's Ditch." Construction began on July 4, 1817, at Rome, New York.

The canal was built largely by hand, using laborers, many of them Irish immigrants, along with horses, oxen, and simple tools. Engineers with little formal training, such as Benjamin Wright and James Geddes, learned on the job and developed methods for clearing forests, removing stumps, and cutting through swampland. The original channel was about 363 miles (584 km) long, 40 feet (12 m) wide, and 4 feet (1.2 m) deep, with 83 locks overcoming an elevation difference of roughly 565 feet (172 m).

The canal officially opened on October 26, 1825, when Clinton traveled from Buffalo to New York City in a ceremonial voyage and poured Lake Erie water into the Atlantic Ocean in the "Wedding of the Waters."

## Economic and social impact

The canal reduced the cost and time of moving freight. Shipping a ton of goods from Buffalo to New York City fell from around $100 to roughly $10, and travel time dropped from weeks to days. Agricultural products from the Midwest flowed east, while manufactured goods and settlers moved west.

New York City surpassed rival ports such as Philadelphia and Boston to become the nation's leading commercial center. Cities along the route, including Syracuse, Rochester, Utica, and Buffalo, grew rapidly. The corridor also became a center of social change, associated with religious revivalism, the women's rights movement, and abolitionism, leading some historians to call western New York the "burned-over district."

## Enlargement and modern use

The canal was enlarged between 1836 and 1862, and from 1905 to 1918 it was replaced by the larger New York State Barge Canal, which incorporated rivers and lakes into its route. Railroads and later highways and the St. Lawrence Seaway reduced commercial traffic in the twentieth century.

Today the canal is used primarily for recreation, including boating, cycling, and tourism along the Erie Canalway Trail. In 2000, Congress designated the Erie Canalway National Heritage Corridor to help preserve it. The canal remains operated by the New York State Canal Corporation.

- DeWitt Clinton
- Great Lakes
- Hudson River
- Transportation in New York

I used to think cars meant freedom. When I was younger, a city seemed to begin where traffic thickened: bright lights, constant motion, engines idling at red lights. A busy street felt important. If everyone was trying to get there, I assumed that was where life was.

I don't see it that way anymore. The older I get, the more I notice what traffic strips out of a place: conversations cut short by sirens, fumes hanging over a summer afternoon, people squeezing along narrow sidewalks while rows of cars sit motionless in the street. When I think about banning cars from city centers, I find myself leaning yes. Not because I dislike cars, but because city centers should belong to people first.

What changed my mind wasn't a statistic, though the case on pollution and safety is strong enough. It was a feeling. In the places I've visited where cars were limited or absent, the change felt immediate. People walked in the street without flinching. Children moved the way children do—suddenly, unpredictably—and nobody seemed to resent them for it. Outdoor tables became places to stay, not little islands in the noise. The city didn't feel empty without cars. It felt lived in.

A city center is not just a route from one place to another. It's where a city sees itself. It's where tourists get their first impression, where office workers buy lunch, where older people cross the street, where protests gather, where strangers become a crowd. When that space is given over to vehicles, it says something bleak about what we value. We choose speed over encounter, convenience over community.

Still, banning cars from city centers is not simple. Some objections are obvious, and some are serious. Disabled people, delivery drivers, emergency services, and commuters coming from places with weak public transit can't be brushed aside. Small businesses may worry about losing customers. Any policy that ignores those realities will feel less like progress than punishment.

So I don't think a ban should be absolute. It should be planned well, with exemptions, dependable public transit, better cycling infrastructure, and clear rules for deliveries and access. The point is not to punish drivers. It's to decide what kind of city life we want to make possible.

Cars are useful. But city centers are too important to shape around them. If we take cars out of those spaces carefully, fairly, and with real alternatives in place, we may find that what looked like a sacrifice is actually a return: cleaner air, quieter streets, and the sense that the center of a city belongs to the people in it.

I still remember walking into my local public library as a child and feeling that I had found a place unlike any other. It was quiet without feeling rigid. It felt full not just of books, but of possibility. I could not have explained then what the library meant to me, but I knew I was welcome there without having to buy anything, prove anything, or be anything in particular. I have carried that feeling with me ever since, and it is part of why I still care so much about public libraries.

Now that almost any fact can be pulled up on a phone in seconds, it is easy to think of libraries as pleasant leftovers from another era. If books can be delivered to your door and articles can be found with a search, what is the library for? To me, the answer is straightforward: a public library does far more than hold information. It gives people access to knowledge, a place to be, and a visible sense of shared life.

What matters most is that a library remains one of the few places that is truly public. So much of daily life now depends on spending money just to remain somewhere. Cafés, stores, and entertainment spaces all come with an unstated cost. A library asks only that people respect the space and the people in it. You can sit, read, think, learn, or just rest. That kind of openness is unusual, and it says something good about a community that chooses to preserve it.

Libraries also matter because access to information is far less equal than people like to assume. Not everyone has dependable internet, a quiet place at home, up-to-date technology, or money for books and subscriptions. The public library helps close those gaps. It offers computers, internet access, job search help, research support, language classes, and educational programs. For a student, it can be a place to study. For someone looking for work, it can be where a résumé gets written and sent. For an immigrant, it can be a first point of connection. For someone who is lonely, it can be a place that feels less isolating.

I also value libraries because they make room for a slower, less directed kind of discovery. Online, algorithms keep steering us toward what they think we already want. In a library, you can wander. You can pull a book from a shelf because the title catches you off guard, or because it happens to sit beside the one you came to find. That kind of chance discovery can change what a person reads, studies, or even imagines for their own life. Libraries remind us that learning is not just about speed. It is also about curiosity.

More than anything, public libraries matter because they express a democratic idea: knowledge should not be reserved for people who can pay for it. A library quietly argues against exclusion. It treats stories, facts, history, imagination, and opportunity as things meant to be shared.

That is why libraries still feel necessary to me. They are not relics. They are working expressions of what a community owes its people. At their best, they show that a town or city is stronger when it keeps a place where anyone can walk in and begin to grow.
